introSummary: IB English tutors help students in Grade 6 through Grade 12 handle two demands at once: close reading under IB command terms, and the written or oral output the syllabus grades — Paper 1 commentary, Paper 2 essays, the Individual Oral, the HL Essay. Searching for a tutor usually means one of three things: a Literature or Language and Literature gap, IA or IO anxiety before a deadline, or marks slipping against the criteria. IB Gram matches a subject-qualified tutor to the level and paper mix your school teaches, online worldwide or in person depending on availability.

contentBlocks.heading: What Changes in IB English Between Grade 6 and Grade 12
contentBlocks.body: A Grade 6 student reading a short story for MYP Language and Literature is being trained in something specific: noticing how a writer's choices create meaning, and saying so using the vocabulary IB calls command terms — analyse, evaluate, examine, justify. That habit does not appear on its own. It gets built session by session, usually through annotation drills a class of twenty-five rarely has time for. By Grade 11 and 12, the same habit has to carry weight under exam pressure: a Paper 1 guided literary analysis done cold, in fifty minutes, on a text the student has never seen. Students who struggle at DP level are frequently repeating a Grade 8 or 9 gap nobody closed — weak textual evidence, a habit of summarising plot instead of arguing a point, or discomfort with unseen text under time pressure. This is why a tutor search that starts in Grade 11 sometimes moves faster than one that starts earlier: the problem is more visible, even if it took years to form. And it is why a family looking earlier, in Grade 7 or 8, should treat that as an advantage rather than jump straight to exam drilling. What matters when choosing a tutor is less about credentials on paper and more about whether the tutor can name, precisely, which of these habits is missing in your child's writing right now, with a plan for that specific gap rather than a generic revision pack.
items: Command terms: analyse, evaluate, examine, justify, discuss
MYP Language and Literature builds the habit DP later tests under pressure
A Grade 11 gap is often a Grade 8 habit never corrected
Look for a tutor who names the specific gap, not a generic pack

contentBlocks.heading: Inside the IB English Syllabus: Papers, the IO and the HL Essay
contentBlocks.body: IB English at Diploma level runs as two related but separate courses: Language A: Literature, built entirely around literary texts, and Language A: Language and Literature, which mixes literary and non-literary text types — adverts, speeches, editorials — with literature. Both are offered at Higher Level and Standard Level, and the difference is not just more reading at HL. It is an HL Essay of 1,200 to 1,500 words on independent literary analysis, plus deeper comparative range across Paper 2. Paper 1 asks for a guided analysis of unseen text; Paper 2 asks for a comparative essay across two studied works, written from memory, no text in the room. The Individual Oral sits apart from both papers: a recorded fifteen-minute conversation linking a global issue to two works, assessed against its own criteria for understanding, analysis, focus and organisation, and language. A tutor who is strong on Paper 2 essay structure is not automatically strong on IO delivery, which is closer to spoken argument than written prose, or on HL Essay research skills, which reward independent source use IB is strict about crediting properly. Before committing to a tutor, it is worth asking directly which of these four components — Paper 1, Paper 2, IO, HL Essay — they actually teach well, rather than assuming general English tutoring covers all four equally.
items: Language A: Literature vs Language A: Language and Literature
HL Essay: 1,200-1,500 words, independent literary analysis
Paper 1: unseen guided analysis; Paper 2: comparative essay, closed text
Individual Oral: recorded, 15 minutes, its own assessment criteria

contentBlocks.heading: From MYP to the Diploma: Where Grade 6 to 12 Fits
contentBlocks.body: IB Gram works with families from Grade 6 to Grade 12, which in practice spans two different programmes with different assessment logic. MYP Language and Literature, roughly Grade 6 through Grade 10, is assessed against four criteria — analysing, organising, producing text, and using language — set by the school within IB's broader framework, and criterion-related rather than norm-referenced: a student is measured against a fixed standard, not ranked against classmates. The Diploma Programme, Grade 11 and 12, narrows into the paper-and-IO structure described above, run against IB's own external moderation. The two do not always transition smoothly. A student who scored well against MYP criteria can still find DP's timed, closed-book Paper 2 unfamiliar territory, because MYP allows more scaffolding and choice of text than DP's fixed exam conditions. Concept-based learning threads through both programmes — students are expected to connect a text to bigger ideas like identity, culture or power, not just comprehend it — and academic honesty rules apply from MYP onward, which matters directly for any tutor helping with an essay or IA: guidance on structure and argument is normal support, writing content that gets submitted as the student's own is not, and a tutor who blurs that line is a liability, not a help. Internal assessment and coursework deadlines are set by each individual school, not by IB centrally, so a tutor working to a generic calendar is working from an assumption rather than your school's actual dates.
items: MYP Language and Literature: roughly Grade 6-10, four assessment criteria
DP English: Grade 11-12, external paper-and-IO structure
Concept-based learning runs through both programmes
Academic honesty limits apply to any tutor helping with an IA or essay

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home or Hybrid: Which Suits an English Tutor
contentBlocks.body: Online tutoring is the default for IB English for one plain reason: subject depth matters more here than proximity. A Language A: Literature specialist who knows the IO criteria cold is worth more than a generalist English tutor who happens to live two streets away, and online access means that specialist is available regardless of which city, or which country, the family is in — sessions run in the family's own time zone, wherever the school itself is based. Home tutoring still has a real place. Younger students, particularly in the MYP years, often concentrate better with a tutor physically in the room, without a screen and its notifications competing for attention, and annotating a shared paper copy of a text is still easier face to face than over a shared screen. Home tutoring depends on a suitable tutor being available for in-person sessions in that city, which is not guaranteed the way online availability is. Hybrid plans are common for exam years: weekly online sessions for regular paper practice, with occasional in-person sessions timed around a mock exam or IA deadline, when working through handwritten annotation together in the same room is worth the scheduling effort. None of these is objectively correct. A Grade 7 student new to annotation may do better in person; a Grade 12 student refining Paper 2 timing technique with a specific specialist may do better online with that exact tutor, wherever they are.
items: Online: widest access to subject specialists, any time zone
Home: suits younger students, depends on local tutor availability
Hybrid: online weekly, in-person around mocks or IA deadlines
Match the mode to the student's age and exam stage, not habit

contentBlocks.heading: How a Tutor Gets Matched to Your Child's Syllabus
contentBlocks.body: Matching starts with specifics, not a general request for an English tutor. IB Gram asks for the course (Literature or Language and Literature), the level (HL or SL), the grade, and what the family actually needs help with right now — IO preparation, IA or coursework structure, past-paper technique, or general syllabus support across the year. That detail changes which tutors are even considered; a tutor strong on HL Essay supervision is not the right match for a Grade 6 student building basic annotation habits. Once a shortlist is drawn up, subject background and relevant exam-board familiarity are checked against what the family described, not against a generic English-teaching resume. A first session is diagnostic rather than instructional: the tutor reviews recent work, asks the student to talk through a short passage using command terms, and identifies where the specific gap sits — evidence use, structure, time management, or confidence under exam conditions. From that, a plan gets set for the following four to six weeks, with concrete, checkable goals rather than a vague promise of improvement. Fit is reviewed early and honestly. If a tutor's teaching style and the student's learning style do not click within the first few sessions, this is treated as normal and correctable, not as failure on either side, and a different tutor is proposed rather than persisting through a mismatch that scheduling logic alone will not fix.
items: Matching starts from course, level, grade and current need
First session is diagnostic: recent work, a command-terms discussion, gap identified
A four-to-six-week plan follows, with checkable goals
Mismatch in the first sessions gets a tutor change, not persistence

contentBlocks.heading: Home Tutoring Reach: City by City, Subject to Availability
contentBlocks.body: Online tutoring removes geography from the equation almost entirely: a specialist Language A: Literature tutor can work with a student in one time zone from a base in another, and most IB English tutoring on the platform runs this way by default. Home and hybrid sessions are different, because they depend on a suitable tutor actually being reachable within a family's city. Families researching a tutor from cities such as Delhi, Bangalore, Chennai, Ahmedabad, Chandigarh, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Coimbatore, Dehradun, Faridabad, Ghaziabad or Greater Noida can request home or hybrid tutoring, and availability is checked at the point of enquiry rather than promised in advance — a family in one part of a city may have several suitable tutors within reasonable travel distance, while a family in a less-served pocket of the same city may find only one, or none, which is exactly where online tutoring becomes the more reliable option rather than a fallback. This is not a limitation specific to English; it is true of home tutoring generally, and IB English is no exception. What is specific to English is that the subject rewards continuity with one tutor across a full academic year far more than a subject like Mathematics does, because essay and IO feedback compounds — a tutor who has already read three of a student's essays gives sharper feedback than one reading their first. That continuity argument favours choosing an online-capable specialist match over a nearby but less well-matched local tutor, in most cases.
items: Online tutoring is available regardless of city or time zone
Home and hybrid depend on a suitable tutor being reachable locally
Enquiries from cities including Delhi, Bangalore and Chennai are checked individually
Continuity with one tutor across the year matters more in English than in some other subjects

contentBlocks.heading: What Gets Checked Before a Tutor Is Introduced to You
contentBlocks.body: Vetting an English tutor is not the same exercise as vetting a Maths or Physics tutor, and it should not be treated as one. Subject qualification is checked first — a genuine background in English literature or literary studies, not simply fluency in the language, since teaching Paper 2 comparative structure is a different skill from correcting grammar. Exam-board familiarity is checked next: has the tutor actually taught to IB's specific command terms and criteria, or is their experience with a different syllabus being adapted on the fly? This distinction matters more in English than in most subjects, because IB's assessment criteria — organisation, language, analysis, understanding — are worded specifically and marked against IB's own descriptors, not against generic essay-writing standards a tutor may have learned elsewhere. Teaching history is reviewed where available, along with how a tutor describes their own approach to feedback, since vague answers here, such as 'I help students improve', are a weaker signal than a tutor who can describe, concretely, how they mark a mock Paper 1 or structure an IO practice session. None of this produces a guarantee of results; no responsible tutoring platform can honestly offer one. But it does mean a family is not starting from a cold search and a set of unverifiable claims. What a parent should expect at introduction is a short account of the tutor's relevant background and how it maps onto the specific need described at matching.
items: Subject qualification in English literature or literary studies, not just fluency
Exam-board familiarity with IB's own command terms and criteria
Concrete description of feedback method, not a vague claim
No guaranteed outcome: verification reduces risk, it does not remove it

contentBlocks.heading: Working Alongside Your School, Not Around It
contentBlocks.body: A tutor's job in IB English is to support what the school is already teaching, not to replace it or run a separate curriculum alongside it. That starts with the basics: the tutor should ask what text list the school has set, which criteria version the school is using for IA or coursework, and when the school's own internal deadlines fall, since IB does not set these centrally and one school's mock exam timetable can differ from another's by weeks. A tutor who ignores this and works from a generic syllabus overview is not saving time; they are creating a second, conflicting version of the course for the student to reconcile. Academic honesty is the other place this matters directly. Any IA, coursework or HL Essay support has to stay on the right side of a clear line: helping a student understand a mark scheme, structure an argument, or revise their own draft is legitimate tutoring; writing content that gets submitted as the student's own work is not, and schools do check for this. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and is not officially affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, and does not claim to speak for any individual school's policies or specific text choices. Families should treat the school as the authority on curriculum specifics, and the tutor as support built around whatever that school has actually set.
items: Ask early which text list, criteria version and internal deadlines the school uses
A tutor should adapt to the school's syllabus, not run a parallel one
Academic honesty: help with structure and argument, not submitted content
IB Gram is independent, not affiliated with IB, Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel

contentBlocks.heading: Where Tutoring Helps and Where It Cannot
contentBlocks.body: Tutoring changes how a student prepares, argues and revises. It does not change how IB assesses. No tutor, however well matched, can promise a specific grade, a 7, or a fixed point improvement, and any that does is making a claim the assessment system does not support — final marks depend on external moderation the tutor has no access to. What a good match reliably delivers is more modest and more checkable: sharper use of textual evidence, a clearer sense of what each command term is actually asking for, faster and more structured Paper 1 and Paper 2 practice, and an IO the student can deliver without reading from notes. Four weeks in, a parent should be able to see concrete change, not a report card, but a visible shift in how the student annotates a text, plans an essay under time pressure, or talks about a work out loud. If that shift is not visible by then, it is worth raising directly with the tutor rather than assuming more time will fix it; sometimes it will, sometimes the match itself needs revisiting. One honest limitation: a tutor starting with a Grade 12 student three weeks before the May session can improve exam technique meaningfully, but cannot rebuild three years of reading habits in that window, and a family in that position is better served by tightly scoped exam-technique sessions than by a plan that promises more than the timeline allows.
items: No guaranteed grades or point improvements; moderation is external
Checkable four-week signals: evidence use, essay planning, oral delivery
Raise a stalled match directly rather than waiting it out
Starting weeks before exams limits scope to technique, not habit-building

contentBlocks.heading: Starting With a First Session
contentBlocks.body: Getting started does not require deciding on a mode, a schedule or a tutor in advance. It starts with a short description of the course, level, grade and current concern, whether that is a looming IO, a slipping Paper 2 score, or simply a Grade 7 student who needs steadier reading habits before DP arrives. From there, a shortlist is drawn against subject background and exam-board familiarity, availability is confirmed for online, home or hybrid depending on the family's city and preference, and a first diagnostic session is arranged. That first session is where the real decision gets made, not before it, on the strength of a profile alone. Families in a city with several IB schools nearby often assume home tutoring will be easy to arrange; sometimes it is, and sometimes the better-matched specialist for that exact course and level is only available online, which is worth knowing before ruling it out on principle. Either way, nothing about starting the process commits a family to a long-term plan before the fit has actually been tested in a real session. A four-to-six-week review point follows naturally, by which time the direction should be visibly working, or worth adjusting.
items: Describe course, level, grade and current concern to start
Shortlist checked against subject background and exam-board familiarity
First session is diagnostic, not a commitment
Review at four to six weeks; adjust the plan or the tutor if needed

faqs.question: How much do IB English tutors charge?
faqs.answer: Fees vary by tutor experience, level (HL typically costs a little more than SL because of the HL Essay and extra reading load), and whether sessions are online or in person, with online usually more cost-efficient since travel is not being charged for. IB Gram does not fix a single rate; a specific quote is confirmed once a tutor is matched to your course and grade, and depends on tutor availability and session frequency. Ask for per-session and package pricing before committing, and confirm whether IA or IO-focused sessions are billed the same as regular syllabus sessions.

faqs.question: Does online IB English tutoring actually work for essay writing and the Individual Oral?
faqs.answer: Yes, for most students, with one caveat: annotation-heavy early sessions can feel less natural on screen than with a shared paper text. Essay structure, Paper 1 and Paper 2 technique, and IO rehearsal all translate well online, and the IO itself is a recorded conversation, so practising it over video is close to the real format. What matters more than online versus in person is whether the tutor gives specific, written feedback the student can revisit, rather than only verbal comments during the session that get forgotten by the next one.

faqs.question: What if my child's tutor and their learning style just do not click?
faqs.answer: This is common enough that IB Gram treats it as routine, not as a failure to fix quietly. Raise it within the first two or three sessions rather than waiting through a term hoping it improves, since early mismatch rarely resolves on its own in a subject like English where feedback style matters. A replacement tutor is matched based on what specifically did not work, whether that is pacing, feedback style, or subject emphasis, so the same mismatch is not repeated. There is no penalty for asking, and doing it early costs far less time than persisting.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the Individual Assessment or coursework without crossing academic honesty rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a clear boundary. A tutor can explain the assessment criteria, discuss structure, review a draft and point out where argument or evidence is weak, and that is legitimate support most schools expect students to seek. A tutor writing content, sentences or analysis that gets submitted as the student's own is not permitted, and schools do check for this. If a tutor ever offers to write part of an assignment, treat that as a signal to end the arrangement, not as a convenience worth accepting.

faqs.question: My child is starting IB English tutoring three months before the May session — is that too late?
faqs.answer: Not too late for meaningful improvement in exam technique, timing and command-term precision, but it is too late to rebuild years of reading habits from scratch. Three months is enough time for focused Paper 1 and Paper 2 practice, IO rehearsal, and mark-scheme familiarity to lift performance visibly. What it will not do is turn a student who rarely reads closely into one with deep literary instinct by May. Being honest about that distinction upfront helps set a realistic, achievable plan rather than an overreaching one.

faqs.question: Is there a difference between tutoring for Language A: Literature and Language A: Language and Literature?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it affects who should tutor your child. Literature focuses entirely on literary texts and closer textual analysis across a longer reading list. Language and Literature adds non-literary text types, such as adverts, opinion pieces and speeches, and asks students to compare how meaning is constructed differently across text types, a distinct skill from literary analysis alone. A tutor strong in one is not automatically strong in the other, so confirm which course your child is actually studying before matching, not just that they need general 'English' help.

faqs.question: Do you offer home tutoring in my city, or only online?
faqs.answer: Both, depending on tutor availability where you are. Online is available everywhere and worldwide, in your own time zone, and is the default for most families because it gives access to specialists regardless of location. Home tutoring is checked city by city; families researching from Delhi, Bangalore, Chennai, Ahmedabad and other cities can request it, and IB Gram confirms whether a suitably matched tutor is reachable for in-person sessions before committing either way. A hybrid mix of both is common for exam years.

faqs.question: What actually happens in the first session?
faqs.answer: The first session is diagnostic, not a straight jump into new content. The tutor reviews recent essays or IA drafts, asks the student to talk through a short passage using IB command terms, and identifies specifically where marks are being lost, whether that is weak evidence, unclear structure, timing under exam pressure, or nerves around speaking for the IO. From that, a four-to-six-week plan is set with concrete goals, so both the parent and the tutor have something specific to check progress against, rather than a vague sense of getting better.

faqs.question: My child is only in Grade 6 or 7 — is it too early for a tutor?
faqs.answer: No, and in some ways it is the easier stage to fix habits in, because MYP marking allows more time and scaffolding than DP's timed exams do later. Early tutoring at this stage usually focuses on annotation, using command terms accurately, and building comfort with unfamiliar texts, rather than exam drilling. Students who build these habits before Grade 10 tend to find the jump into DP's Paper 1 and Paper 2 format less jarring, since the underlying skill was already there before the exam pressure was added on top.

faqs.question: What happens if there is no visible progress after a few weeks?
faqs.answer: Raise it directly with the tutor at the four-week mark rather than waiting until a mock exam reveals it. Ask specifically what has changed in the student's evidence use, essay planning or oral confidence, since these are checkable even before grades move. Sometimes the fix is a change in feedback style or session frequency; sometimes the tutor genuinely is not the right match, and a change is made without treating it as wasted time. What should not happen is continuing for months on the assumption that more of the same will eventually work.

heroTitle: IB Individuals and Societies Tutoring, Wherever Your School Is
heroSubtitle: For Grade 6 to Grade 12 students working through History, Geography, Economics, Psychology or Business Management under the IB syllabus, matched with a tutor who understands command terms, criterion-related assessment and the IA process, online in your own time zone, or at home where a tutor is nearby.
introSummary: IB Individuals and Societies tutors help students across History, Geography, Economics, Business Management, Psychology and Global Politics, the Group 3 subjects most IB Diploma and MYP students choose at least one of. Finding the right one usually means finding someone who has actually marked or taught to IB criteria, not just the subject content. IB Gram matches families with tutors for online sessions worldwide, or home and hybrid sessions where a tutor happens to be local, covering Grade 6 to Grade 12, with IA guidance, past-paper practice and mock preparation built around each school's own internal deadlines.

contentBlocks.heading: What a Screen Can Do Better Than a Local Tutor, and What It Can't
contentBlocks.body:
Individuals and Societies is where IB students often first meet real argument-based writing: an essay that has to weigh evidence, acknowledge a counter-view, and use command terms like 'evaluate' or 'discuss' precisely rather than loosely. A tutor teaching History, Geography, Economics, Business Management, Psychology or Global Politics needs subject depth most generalist tutors do not have, and that is exactly where online tutoring earns its keep: a family in a smaller city, or in a country with few IB schools nearby, can still reach a tutor who has actually taught the Paper 2 source-based question or the IA research proposal at this level. Geography stops mattering when the lesson is a shared screen and a set of mark schemes.

Where online falls short is with younger or easily distracted learners, particularly early in MYP, where a tutor sitting beside the student to build note-taking habits does more than any video call. It also struggles when a student needs the tutor to physically annotate a printed past paper mid-session, though most tutors now work around this with shared documents. IB Gram runs both models side by side rather than picking one as universally better: online where subject specialism matters more than proximity, home tutoring where the student's age, attention span or study habits matter more, and hybrid where a family wants both across the two-year DP cycle.

History, Geography, Economics, Business Management, Psychology, Global Politics
Online sessions run in the family's own time zone
Home tutoring depends on tutor availability in the city
Hybrid plans combine both across a term

contentBlocks.heading: How the Subject Changes from MYP to the Diploma
contentBlocks.body:
Individuals and Societies is not one fixed course; it changes shape as a student moves through the IB. In the Middle Years Programme it is usually a single broad subject blending history, geography, economics and civics, assessed against four MYP criteria rather than an external exam. By the Diploma Programme, a student picks one specific Group 3 subject, at Higher or Standard Level, and the assessment becomes external: Paper 1 source or data-response questions, Paper 2 essay questions, and for many of these subjects an internally assessed piece of coursework or an IA built around a research question the student designs themselves.

This matters for tutoring because a tutor who is excellent at MYP Individuals and Societies is not automatically the right fit for DP Economics HL, and the reverse is just as true. A parent asking for help with 'Individuals and Societies' at Grade 11 needs someone fluent in that specific DP subject's command terms and mark bands, not a generalist. IB Gram treats the MYP-to-DP transition as a genuine hinge point: tutoring support around Grade 9 and 10 focuses on academic writing habits and source evaluation that will matter regardless of which DP subject gets chosen, while Grade 11 and 12 support narrows immediately to the chosen subject's syllabus, its own IA structure and its own exam sessions in May or November.
items: MYP: broad, criterion-assessed, no external exam
DP: one Group 3 subject at HL or SL
Paper 1 and Paper 2 external assessment
IA or coursework specific to the subject chosen
May and November examination sessions

contentBlocks.heading: Where a Tutor Can Actually Reach You
contentBlocks.body:
Because Individuals and Societies tutoring runs mostly online, geography is less of a constraint than it once was. A student in a city with only two or three IB World Schools can still be matched with a tutor who has taught the exact DP subject for years, working entirely over video call in the family's own time zone. Online only removes the distance problem, though, not the time-zone one, and families searching across very different time zones from their tutor should expect scheduling to take a few tries before it settles.

Home tutoring works differently: it depends entirely on whether a suitable tutor happens to live and travel within a reasonable radius of the family, which IB Gram cannot promise in advance for every city. In practice this tends to work out more easily in cities with a larger number of IB and IGCSE schools clustered together, such as Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Chennai, Delhi, Chandigarh or Coimbatore, where enough tutors are active locally that a reasonable match usually exists; it is genuinely harder in smaller towns, where online is often the only realistic option and families should plan for that rather than hold out for a home tutor who may not exist nearby. Cities such as Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Dehradun, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Greater Noida sit somewhere between the two, with home tutoring possible but subject to which tutors are active there at the time a family enquires.
items: Online tutoring: available everywhere, limited only by time zone
Home tutoring: subject to tutor availability in that city
Larger IB/IGCSE hubs make home matching easier
Smaller towns usually rely on online sessions
Hybrid support possible where both exist

contentBlocks.heading: The Six Subjects Families Usually Mean by 'Individuals and Societies'
contentBlocks.body:
When a parent searches for an Individuals and Societies tutor, they usually mean one of six DP subjects: History, Geography, Economics, Business Management, Psychology or Global Politics. Each has its own command terms, its own paper structure and its own IA or coursework format, and treating them as interchangeable is the single most common mistake families make when picking a tutor.

History HL/SL leans on source evaluation and extended essay-style argument across Paper 1, 2 and 3. Geography blends physical and human geography with fieldwork-based internal assessment. Economics is the most quantitative of the group, with real diagrams, data-response questions and a strict command-term hierarchy between 'define', 'explain' and 'evaluate'. Business Management asks students to apply theory to real case studies under exam conditions. Psychology covers biological, cognitive and sociocultural approaches with a research-methods-heavy internal assessment. Global Politics is newer to many schools and leans on current affairs engagement alongside political theory.

A tutor strong in one of these is not automatically strong in another, even though all six sit under the same subject group and share IB's general approach to concept-based learning and academic honesty. IB Gram asks specifically which DP subject a family needs before matching, rather than treating 'Individuals and Societies' as one interchangeable label, because a Geography specialist walking into an Economics data-response paper helps nobody.
items: History: source evaluation, Papers 1-3
Geography: physical/human geography, fieldwork IA
Economics: diagrams, data response, quantitative
Business Management: case-study application
Psychology: research methods, three approaches
Global Politics: current affairs plus theory

contentBlocks.heading: What School Context Changes About Tutoring Support
contentBlocks.body:
IB World Schools vary a great deal in how they teach Individuals and Societies, even within the same subject and level. Some schools front-load IA research skills in Grade 11, leaving Grade 12 almost entirely for exam technique; others spread coursework across both years and expect students to juggle Paper 1 revision alongside a live internal assessment draft. A tutor who does not ask which model the student's school follows will end up teaching to the wrong timeline.

Internal deadlines set by the school, not the IB Organization's own calendar, are usually what actually governs a family's tutoring schedule in any given term. A mock exam set for early December means different preparation than one set for February, even for the same subject and the same May session. IB Gram tutors are briefed to ask for the school's own internal assessment calendar in the first session rather than assuming a generic timeline, because two students in the same DP subject and the same exam session can be at genuinely different stages of their IA depending only on which school they attend.

To be direct about something families sometimes assume incorrectly: IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and is not officially affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel. Nothing on this page should be read as school-endorsed or IB-endorsed; it describes how tutoring support is organised around whatever calendar the student's own school sets.
items: Ask for the school's own internal deadline calendar first
IA timelines vary school to school, not just by subject
Mock exam dates shift preparation priorities
IB Gram is independent, not IB/Cambridge/Pearson Edexcel affiliated

contentBlocks.heading: How a Tutor Actually Gets Matched to a Student
contentBlocks.body:
Matching starts with three questions that matter more than most parents expect: which DP or MYP subject and level, which exam session the student is working toward, and what the school's own internal assessment calendar looks like. A tutor is then proposed based on subject-specific teaching or marking background in that exact course, not a general 'humanities tutor' label.

The first session is diagnostic rather than instructional in the fullest sense: the tutor reviews recent essays or IA drafts, checks how the student is applying command terms, and identifies whether the gap is content knowledge, exam technique, or writing structure, since these three need different fixes and get conflated far too often. A student who 'knows the content but loses marks' usually has a technique problem, not a knowledge one, and the first session is where that distinction gets made rather than assumed.

From there, a short-term plan is set, usually four to six weeks, with specific, checkable goals rather than a vague aim to 'improve'. Around week four, progress gets reviewed against those original goals: has the essay structure improved, is source evaluation stronger, has the IA draft moved forward. If it has not, the honest response is to change approach or occasionally change tutor, not to keep repeating the same sessions and hoping for a different result. Fit between tutor and student communication style matters as much as subject knowledge, and IB Gram treats a mismatch as fixable rather than something families must simply live with.
items: Subject, level and exam session identified upfront
First session is diagnostic, not instructional
Four to six week plan with checkable goals
Week four review against those specific goals
Tutor changed if fit or progress isn't there

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home and Hybrid, Compared Honestly
contentBlocks.body:
Online tutoring for Individuals and Societies works well precisely because so much of the subject is discussion, essay feedback and mark-scheme analysis, none of which needs to happen in person. A shared document with a marked-up past paper, a video call, and a tutor who has actually taught the DP subject in question covers most of what a student needs, and it means subject specialism can be prioritised over geography.

Home tutoring earns its place for a different reason: younger students, particularly in MYP, often need someone physically present to build consistent study habits, and some students simply concentrate better away from a screen. Its limit is availability. Not every city has enough active tutors for every subject and level combination, and traffic or distance can make an otherwise good match impractical for a weekly session.

Hybrid plans try to take the better half of each: a weekly online session for subject teaching and IA guidance, with an occasional in-person session before a mock exam or a major coursework deadline, scheduled when it is actually useful rather than as a fixed ratio. None of these three is objectively best. A Grade 12 student six weeks from a May exam usually gets more from focused online Paper 2 practice than from switching modes; a Grade 7 student just starting Individuals and Societies may benefit far more from a present adult building habits than from any amount of online polish. The honest answer to 'which mode is best' is: it depends on the student's age, the subject stage, and what a family can actually sustain week after week, not which sounds more premium.
items: Online: best for subject specialism and exam technique
Home: best for younger learners building habits
Hybrid: online teaching plus occasional in-person sessions
Mode choice depends on age and exam proximity
No single mode is universally better

contentBlocks.heading: What a Parent Should Reasonably Expect After Four Weeks
contentBlocks.body:
No responsible tutor can promise a grade, a 7, or a fixed percentage improvement, and any that does should be treated with suspicion rather than relief. What can be reasonably expected after about four weeks of consistent sessions is narrower and more useful: an essay structure that follows the command term instead of drifting into general description, source or data analysis that goes one level deeper than before, and an IA draft that has moved from a vague topic to an actual research question with a plan attached.

Progress in Individuals and Societies is often slower to show than in a subject like Mathematics, because the skill being built is argument quality, and argument quality improves in increments that are easy to miss week to week and only obvious when a parent compares an essay from week one against week six. Ask to see both. A tutor who cannot point to a specific, concrete change in the student's work by week four, beyond general reassurance that 'things are going well', is a signal worth taking seriously.

It is also fair to expect the reverse to be communicated honestly: if a student started IA planning very late, or if the gap between current level and target level is large for the time remaining before a May or November session, a good tutor says so directly rather than promising a turnaround that the calendar does not support. Starting late narrows what is realistically achievable, and a tutor who pretends otherwise is not doing the family a favour.
items: No grade or score guarantees, ever
Week 1 vs week 6 essay comparison is the honest test
Argument quality improves gradually, not overnight
A late start genuinely limits what's achievable
Tutor should flag risk honestly, not just reassure

contentBlocks.heading: How Tutors Are Checked Before Being Matched
contentBlocks.body:
Every tutor proposed for an Individuals and Societies match is checked against a specific combination of criteria before being offered to a family: subject background in the exact DP or MYP course, familiarity with the IB's command terms and criterion-related mark bands for that subject, and, where possible, direct experience with IA supervision or marking at this level. A tutor's stated experience is checked against what they can actually demonstrate, such as sample feedback on past IA drafts or familiarity with recent past papers, rather than accepted on the strength of a CV line alone.

This matters more in Individuals and Societies than in some other subjects because the assessment criteria reward specific, learnable skills: source evaluation, command-term precision, structured argument. A tutor who cannot demonstrate they teach to those criteria specifically is not much more useful than a well-read family member. Academic honesty is checked too: a tutor who offers to write or substantially rewrite IA content rather than teach the skills behind it is not someone IB Gram continues to work with, since that puts the student's own academic integrity at risk, not just their grade.

Ongoing checks continue after the first match as well. Parent feedback after the diagnostic session and again around the four-week mark feeds back into whether that tutor continues to be recommended for similar students, which is a slower but more honest signal than a one-time credential check could ever be on its own.
items: Subject background verified for the exact DP/MYP course
Command-term and mark-band familiarity checked
IA supervision experience considered where available
No IA ghostwriting; academic honesty enforced
Ongoing parent feedback reviewed after matching

contentBlocks.heading: Getting Started With an Individuals and Societies Tutor
contentBlocks.body:
Starting is simpler than most families expect, and does not require deciding on a mode or a long-term commitment upfront. It begins with naming the specific subject, level and exam session, since 'Individuals and Societies' alone is not enough for a good match, as covered earlier. From there, a short conversation about the school's own internal deadlines and the student's current stage, whether that is early MYP habit-building or a Grade 12 student six weeks from finals, determines who gets proposed.

A first session gets scheduled to diagnose rather than commit to months of tutoring immediately. Many families start with a short block, four to six weeks, specifically so the week-four review has something concrete to assess before anyone commits further. This also protects against the common mistake of locking into a long-term arrangement with a tutor who turns out to be a poor fit, subject-wise or otherwise.

For families outside a major IB hub, expect the first proposed match to be online by default, since that is where subject depth is most reliably available regardless of city. For families in a city with a denser IB and IGCSE presence, a home or hybrid option may be offered alongside the online one, subject to which tutors are actually active there when the enquiry comes in. Either way, the process starts with a specific ask, not a general one, and gets more useful the more specific that ask is.
items: Name the exact subject, level and exam session
Share the school's internal IA/deadline calendar
Start with a 4-6 week diagnostic block
Online offered by default; home/hybrid where available
Review and adjust at week four before continuing

faqs.question: Is online tutoring actually enough for a subject like History or Economics at DP level?
faqs.answer: For most students, yes, because the bulk of the work, essay feedback, mark-scheme analysis, source evaluation and IA guidance, happens through discussion and shared documents rather than anything that needs a physical room. Where online genuinely struggles is with younger students who need someone present to build consistent study habits, and with families who prefer face-to-face accountability. For a Grade 11 or 12 student preparing for Paper 1, 2 or 3, online tutoring with a tutor who has actually taught that exact DP subject usually matters more than whether the session happens in person.

faqs.question: What happens if my child's Individuals and Societies IA is already overdue at school?
faqs.answer: A tutor can still help, but the plan changes. Instead of building the research question from scratch over several weeks, the focus becomes triage: identifying what the school will actually accept given the delay, tightening the existing draft fast, and being honest about how much the mark can realistically improve given the compressed timeline. Starting this late limits what's achievable, and a tutor who promises a full turnaround in a week or two is not being straight with you. It is still worth doing; the goal simply shifts from 'best possible IA' to 'strongest achievable one in the time left'.

faqs.question: How much does IB Individuals and Societies tutoring cost?
faqs.answer: Fees depend on the tutor's experience, the subject and level (HL work with an experienced tutor typically costs more than SL), whether sessions are online, home or hybrid, and how many sessions a week the family wants. Rather than one fixed number, IB Gram shares tutor-specific fee options once a subject, level and exam session are confirmed, so the quote actually reflects the match rather than a generic rate card. It is reasonable to ask for options at more than one price point before committing, and to compare what is included, session length, IA review, past-paper marking, before deciding.

faqs.question: Can I change tutors if it isn't working out?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is worth doing sooner rather than later if the fit clearly is not there. A mismatch usually shows up within the first two or three sessions, either in communication style or in the tutor's grip on the specific DP subject, and there is no benefit to pushing through a term hoping it improves on its own. IB Gram treats a tutor change as a normal part of finding the right match, not a failure, and the week-four review is designed precisely to catch this early rather than let a poor fit run for months.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram guarantee a grade improvement or a 7?
faqs.answer: No, and any platform or tutor that promises a specific grade should be treated with caution. What tutoring can reasonably deliver is better exam technique, stronger source or data analysis, a more developed IA, and clearer command-term understanding, all of which influence a final grade without guaranteeing one, since a grade also depends on factors outside any tutor's control: the student's own effort, the specific paper set that session, and the school's internal marking. IB Gram focuses on describing the process honestly rather than promising an outcome no one can actually control.

faqs.question: My child is starting IB Individuals and Societies at Grade 6 in the Middle Years Programme. Is tutoring necessary this early?
faqs.answer: Not usually necessary, but it can be useful if a student is struggling specifically with essay structure, source evaluation or the MYP criteria themselves, rather than with content. At this stage tutoring tends to focus on academic writing habits and how to unpack a command term properly, skills that carry forward directly into the Diploma Programme regardless of which subject gets chosen later. Starting this early is optional, not something families should worry about skipping; a student who picks up these habits at Grade 10 or 11 instead can still catch up.

faqs.question: How does tutoring work if my family moves between time zones or countries mid-year?
faqs.answer: Online sessions run in the family's own time zone, so a move mainly affects scheduling rather than continuity, since the same tutor can usually continue if the new time works for both sides. Where a move creates a genuinely awkward time-zone gap, IB Gram can propose a different tutor already working in a compatible window, with a handover covering the IA stage and recent session notes so the student is not starting over. Continuity of subject matter matters more than continuity of tutor in this situation, and that is the priority in a rematch.

faqs.question: What's the difference between Individuals and Societies tutoring and general homework help?
faqs.answer: Homework help gets an assignment finished; Individuals and Societies tutoring at IB level builds the specific skills the criteria actually reward: command-term precision, structured argument, source or data evaluation, and IA research design. A tutor working to IB criteria checks a student's essay against the actual mark bands used in the exam, not just whether the answer sounds reasonable. Over a term, this distinction is usually what separates steady grade progress from a student who completes every assignment but plateaus at the same technique level exam after exam.

faqs.question: Which Individuals and Societies subject should my child actually pick for the Diploma?
faqs.answer: That decision sits with the school and student, not with a tutor, but a diagnostic conversation before subject selection can help: a student strong in quantitative reasoning often does better in Economics, one who enjoys sustained argument and reading often prefers History, and one interested in current affairs may lean toward Global Politics. IB Gram does not push a subject choice; a tutor's role at this stage is to help a family understand what each subject actually demands week to week, HL Economics' data work, History's reading load, before the choice is locked in with the school.

faqs.question: Is a tutor who taught the same subject at another curriculum, like A-Level Economics, good enough for IB Economics?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. IB assesses differently: command terms, criterion-related mark bands, an internally assessed component in some subjects, and concept-based learning that other boards do not structure the same way. Subject knowledge transfers, but exam technique for IB specifically does not, and a tutor unfamiliar with IB's own command-term hierarchy or IA requirements will teach content correctly while still leaving a student unprepared for how IB actually marks. IB Gram checks for IB-specific teaching or marking background, not just subject knowledge from another curriculum, before making a match.

contentBlocks.heading: Three Different Timelines, Three Different Kinds of Help
contentBlocks.body:
Parents arrive at this page for different reasons depending on where they are in the year. Some are here this week because a mock result landed badly and there are three weeks until the next one. Some are planning this month, mapping out revision before internal assessment deadlines close in. And some are thinking a term or a year ahead, choosing a tutor before Grade 11 starts so the working relationship is already solid when coursework season begins.

Each timeline needs something different from a tutor. A this-week problem usually needs targeted paper practice and a clear read on what a mark scheme is actually rewarding, not a full syllabus rebuild. A this-month plan benefits from someone who can sit alongside the IA process, questioning sources and structure before a draft goes to the school. A this-term or this-year decision is really about fit: a tutor whose subject background and working style will hold up over eight or ten months, not just one crisis.

IB Gram asks which of these applies before suggesting a tutor, because the honest answer changes the plan. A student six weeks from the May session needs a different kind of session than one just starting Grade 6. Getting the timeline wrong wastes the first two or three sessions on the wrong problem, which matters when time before an exam session is fixed and cannot be recovered.
items: This week: targeted paper practice and mark-scheme reading
This month: IA structure and source work before a draft is due
This term or year: tutor fit for the full course, not one crisis
Six weeks before May or November needs a different plan than Grade 6

contentBlocks.heading: Where Tutoring Actually Happens
contentBlocks.body:
IB Individuals and Societies tutors on IB Gram work with families in more than one way, and where you are changes which options are realistic. Online tutoring is available worldwide and runs in the family's own time zone, which is the option most families actually use — it means a strong Individuals and Societies tutor is not limited to whoever happens to live nearby. Home tutoring is different: it depends on a tutor being available for in-person sessions in your city, and that varies. In cities such as Bangalore, Chennai, Delhi, Ahmedabad, Chandigarh, Coimbatore, Dehradun and Bhubaneswar, home tutoring can sometimes be arranged, subject to which tutors are currently taking students in that area and how far they can reasonably travel for a weekly session.

This is worth saying plainly: home tutoring is not available everywhere, and pretending otherwise wastes a parent's time on a call that goes nowhere. If a home tutor is not currently available where you are, online is not a downgrade. For a subject built on essay structure, source evaluation and IA feedback, a shared document and a video call cover most of what an in-person session would, and it opens up tutors who specialise specifically in this subject group rather than whoever happens to be local. Hybrid plans, mixing occasional in-person sessions with regular online ones, suit families who want both without depending on one mode entirely.

Home tutoring: depends on tutor availability in your city

Hybrid: occasional in-person sessions plus regular online ones

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home and Hybrid, Compared Honestly
contentBlocks.body:
The honest comparison between online, home and hybrid tutoring depends on the student's age and habits, not on which sounds more serious. Online tutoring gives access to specialist subject tutors regardless of city, which matters more in Individuals and Societies than in some subjects, since a tutor who has actually taught or examined the specific option your school follows is not always available within driving distance. Screen sharing works well for annotating source extracts, building essay plans together and walking through a mark scheme line by line.

Home tutoring suits younger learners more than older ones. A Grade 6 or 7 student building basic source-analysis habits often does better with someone physically in the room, keeping attention on the page rather than the screen. By Grade 11 and 12, most students manage online sessions perfectly well and prefer the flexibility, since there's no travel time cut out of an already tight evening.

Hybrid plans combine both: a fortnightly in-person session for deeper feedback, with weekly online check-ins for pacing and doubt-solving in between. This suits families who want the depth of face-to-face work without needing it every single week, and it is often the more realistic option once school timings and travel are accounted for. None of the three is universally better. The honest answer depends on the student sitting in front of the material, not on which option looks most reassuring on paper.
items: Online: specialist access regardless of city, strong for annotation and mark-scheme work
Home: often better for younger students building basic habits
Hybrid: fortnightly in-person plus weekly online check-ins
Choice should follow the student's age and habits, not assumption

contentBlocks.heading: What Sits Inside the Individuals and Societies Group
contentBlocks.body:
Individuals and Societies covers a group of subjects rather than one fixed syllabus, and schools choose which options they offer, so the group can include historical, geographical, economic, political, psychological or business-focused strands depending on the school. What ties them together at IB level is not content but method: concept-based learning, tight academic honesty rules around sourcing, command terms that specify exactly what a question wants, and criterion-related assessment where marks are awarded against published descriptors rather than a simple right-or-wrong scheme.

This is exactly where a lot of otherwise strong students lose marks, not because they don't know the content, but because they answer the question they wish had been asked rather than the one on the page. A tutor working in this group spends real time on command-term discipline: what 'evaluate' expects that 'describe' does not, and how to structure a response so each paragraph earns marks against the criteria rather than simply adding information.

Because the specific subject and syllabus varies by school, matching starts with naming exactly which option your child studies and which syllabus it follows, so the tutor brought in has actually taught or examined that specific course rather than a neighbouring one that merely sounds similar. Getting this detail right at the start saves a wasted first session.
items: Concept-based learning across the group, not just content recall
Command-term precision: evaluate versus describe versus compare
Criterion-related marking against published descriptors
Academic honesty and correct sourcing built into every response
Matching starts with naming the exact subject option and syllabus

contentBlocks.heading: How a Tutor Match Gets Made
contentBlocks.body:
Matching starts with specifics, not a general request for 'an IB tutor'. A parent tells IB Gram the exact subject option, the grade, the school's syllabus, and what prompted the search, whether that's a mock result, an approaching IA deadline, or simply wanting steady support through to the May or November session. That detail is what separates a useful match from a generic one; a tutor experienced in coursework supervision is not automatically the right fit for someone six weeks from a final paper.

From there, two or three tutors whose subject background and exam-board familiarity match the request are suggested, along with what they focus on and how they usually structure sessions. A first session is diagnostic rather than instructional: the tutor works through a recent piece of the student's work or a past-paper question to see exactly where marks are being lost, not just whether the student 'seems to understand' the topic.

Fees and scheduling are discussed upfront and depend on the tutor's experience, the subject level and how often sessions run. There is no fixed rate that applies to everyone, and any tutor quoting one without knowing the specifics is guessing. If the first tutor is not the right fit after a session or two, IB Gram arranges a different one rather than asking the family to persist with a mismatch out of politeness.
items: Start with the exact subject option, grade and syllabus, not a general request
First session is diagnostic: recent work or a past-paper question, not a lecture
Fees depend on tutor experience, subject level and session frequency
A poor fit after one or two sessions gets reassigned, not persisted with

contentBlocks.heading: Grade 6 Through Grade 12, and What Changes at Each Stage
contentBlocks.body:
Support looks different at each end of Grade 6 to Grade 12. In the MYP years, roughly Grade 6 to Grade 10, the work is about building the underlying skills the DP will later demand: reading a source without taking it at face value, writing a structured paragraph, and understanding why a claim needs evidence rather than just producing one. Tutoring at this stage is often about closing specific gaps, such as one type of source or one style of question, rather than covering an entire syllabus.

By Grade 11 and 12, in the Diploma Programme, the demands sharpen considerably. Internal assessment and coursework carry real weight, deadlines are set by the school rather than negotiable, and exam-style questions reward technique as much as knowledge. Mock exams typically fall a few months before the actual session, and that window is when most families start looking for focused, weekly support rather than occasional help.

Across both stages, the exam calendar matters more than people initially assume. The May and November IB examination sessions set a fixed point that revision has to work backward from, and internal assessment deadlines set by each individual school create earlier checkpoints inside that timeline that a tutor needs to know about specifically, not generically, since missing one has consequences a mock result alone does not.

Grade 11-12 (DP): IA, coursework and exam technique carry real weight
Mock exams typically precede the May or November session by a few months
Each school sets its own internal assessment deadlines inside the exam calendar

contentBlocks.heading: Working Alongside Your Child's School, Not Around It
contentBlocks.body:
IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform. It is not affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International, Pearson Edexcel, or with any individual school, a fact worth stating plainly rather than leaving vague, because plenty of tutoring services blur this line. A tutor's job here is to support what the school is already teaching, not to replace it or run a separate curriculum alongside it.

In practice this means a tutor needs to see what the school has actually set: the specific IA task sheet, the criteria the school is marking against, and the command terms used in recent internal assessments. Two schools teaching the same Individuals and Societies option can still emphasise different things, and a tutor who ignores that and teaches a generic version of the syllabus does the student a disservice, however knowledgeable they are in general.

Where a school's own teacher is generous with feedback and available for questions, tutoring works best as reinforcement: extra practice, a second explanation, more repetitions of exam technique. Where school access is limited, whether from large class sizes or a teacher covering several subjects, tutoring carries more of the load. Either way, a tutor should be asking to see the school's materials early rather than working from a generic outline, because the gap between the two is usually where marks get lost.
items: Independent platform, not affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel
Tutors work from the school's own IA task sheets and marking criteria
Two schools on the same subject option can still differ in emphasis
Tutoring reinforces school teaching; it does not replace it

contentBlocks.heading: What Gets Checked Before a Tutor Is Matched
contentBlocks.body:
Before a tutor is suggested for an Individuals and Societies request, a few specific things get checked, not just a general claim of experience. Subject background comes first: has this person actually studied or taught the specific option in question, or are they a generalist offering to cover it because it falls loosely under humanities. Exam-board familiarity matters almost as much, since someone who has taught the same content for a different board can still miss what a specific mark scheme rewards.

Teaching history is reviewed where available: how long they have worked with IB students specifically, whether that includes IA supervision or just classroom teaching, and what grade levels they are actually comfortable with. A tutor strong with Grade 11 and 12 coursework is not automatically the right choice for a Grade 6 student still building basic paragraph structure, and the reverse is equally true.

None of this is presented as a guarantee of results. No responsible tutor can promise a grade, and any that does should be treated with suspicion. What can be checked and stated honestly is process: subject match, board familiarity, and a track record with the specific grade range requested. That is what gets verified before a name is suggested to a family, and it gets reviewed again if a family reports that a match isn't working out.
items: Subject background: has actually taught or studied the specific option
Exam-board familiarity, not just general subject knowledge
Teaching history with IB students specifically, including IA supervision where relevant
Grade-range fit checked separately from subject fit
No grade or score is ever promised

contentBlocks.heading: What a Parent Should See by Week Four
contentBlocks.body:
By around four weeks, a parent should be able to see something concrete, not just hear that things are going well. That usually means a specific, nameable change: the student catching their own command-term mistakes before being told, a marked improvement in how a source is used as evidence rather than just quoted, or a first-draft essay plan that holds together without the tutor rebuilding it from scratch.

It is fair to ask the tutor directly what they are seeing and where the gap still is. A tutor who cannot answer specifically, four weeks in, either hasn't been paying close attention or is being vague on purpose. Progress in this subject is rarely dramatic in a month; it shows up as fewer repeated mistakes and slightly more independent structure, not a sudden jump in mock scores.

It is also fair to expect an honest answer if progress has not been visible. Sometimes the issue is fit, where a subject-knowledgeable tutor's teaching style simply doesn't suit the student, and sometimes the issue is frequency, where once a week isn't enough given how far behind the student started. Either is fixable, but only if it gets said plainly rather than papered over with reassurance. A family that has not seen any specific change by week four should ask for a straight answer, not another round of general encouragement.
items: A specific, nameable change by week four, not general reassurance
Fewer repeated command-term mistakes; steadier essay-plan structure
Ask the tutor directly what they see and where the gap remains
If there's no visible change, expect a straight answer on fit or frequency

contentBlocks.heading: Starting This Week
contentBlocks.body:
Starting is simpler than most families expect, and it does not require deciding everything upfront. The first step is naming specifics: the exact Individuals and Societies option, the grade, the school's syllabus, and what is actually prompting the search right now, whether that's a mock result, an approaching IA deadline, or wanting a steady tutor in place before Grade 11 begins. From there, IB Gram suggests tutors whose subject background and exam-board familiarity match what was described, along with how they typically structure a first session.

There is no obligation attached to an initial conversation, and no pressure to commit to a long block of sessions before knowing whether the fit actually works. A single diagnostic session is usually enough to tell whether a tutor's style and the student's habits line up, and if they don't, a different tutor gets suggested rather than the family being asked to make do.

Because the May and November sessions and each school's internal assessment deadlines are fixed points that do not move, the honest advice is not to wait for a better time to start. A student six weeks from a mock benefits more from starting today, even imperfectly, than from waiting three more weeks for an ideal moment that rarely arrives on schedule anyway.
items: Name the exact subject option, grade, syllabus and reason for searching
No obligation on the first conversation
One diagnostic session usually shows whether the fit works
Fixed exam dates mean starting late costs real revision time

faqs.question: How much does an IB Individuals and Societies tutor cost?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed rate. Fees depend on the tutor's experience, the specific subject option, the grade level and how many sessions run each week. A Grade 12 tutor experienced in IA supervision generally costs more than support for a Grade 7 student building basic skills. IB Gram shares the specific fee for a suggested tutor before you commit to anything, rather than quoting a generic platform-wide number that wouldn't reflect the actual match. Ask for this upfront on the first call; any tutor unwilling to discuss it plainly before the first session is worth questioning.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring actually work for a subject like this, or is it better in person?
faqs.answer: For Individuals and Societies specifically, online works well because most of the actual work, annotating a source, building an essay plan, walking through a mark scheme, happens on a shared screen rather than needing physical presence. Grade 11 and 12 students generally manage this comfortably. Younger students, roughly Grade 6 to 8, sometimes focus better with a tutor physically in the room, which is why home tutoring is offered where a tutor happens to be available locally. Neither is universally better; it depends on the student's age and how they concentrate.

faqs.question: Can I get a home tutor, or is it online only?
faqs.answer: Home tutoring can be arranged in cities where a suitable tutor is currently available and able to travel for weekly sessions, which has included cities such as Bangalore, Chennai, Delhi, Ahmedabad and Chandigarh, though availability shifts as tutors' own schedules change. It is not available everywhere, and IB Gram will say so directly rather than promising a home tutor and leaving you waiting. Where a home tutor isn't currently available near you, online tutoring with a specialist in this exact subject option is usually the stronger alternative anyway, not a fallback.

faqs.question: What happens if the tutor and my child don't get along?
faqs.answer: This gets addressed directly rather than smoothed over. If a tutor's style, pace or manner isn't working after a session or two, IB Gram arranges a different tutor rather than asking the family to persist through a mismatch for the sake of continuity. It helps to say specifically what isn't working, too fast, too much lecturing, not enough practice questions, because that detail shapes who gets suggested next. A change in tutor partway through a term is common enough that it shouldn't feel like an admission of failure on the student's part.

faqs.question: How is a tutor for IA support different from one for general revision?
faqs.answer: IA supervision needs a tutor who understands the specific criteria your school is marking against and can question a draft's structure and sourcing without writing it for the student, since academic honesty rules make that distinction important. General revision support leans more on past-paper practice, command-term drilling and closing content gaps ahead of a mock or the May or November session. Some tutors do both well; others specialise in one. Naming which kind of help is actually needed, rather than asking generally for an IB tutor, gets a more accurate match on the first attempt.

faqs.question: My child is only in Grade 6 — is it too early for a subject tutor?
faqs.answer: Not at all, though the focus at this stage looks different from DP-level tutoring. In the MYP years, roughly Grade 6 to Grade 10, the work is usually about building specific skills, reading a source critically, structuring a paragraph, using evidence rather than just stating an opinion, that the Diploma Programme will later assume are already solid. Starting early on a specific weak spot is often more efficient than waiting until Grade 11 and trying to fix the same gap under exam pressure with far less time to spare.

faqs.question: What if there's no real progress after a few weeks?
faqs.answer: Ask directly what the tutor has actually seen change, and expect a specific answer rather than general reassurance. Real progress in this subject usually shows as fewer repeated command-term mistakes and steadier essay structure, not a sudden jump in scores within a month. If nothing specific can be pointed to by around week four, the honest next step is examining whether the issue is fit, frequency, or something the school itself needs to address, and IB Gram will help work out which, rather than simply continuing the same sessions and hoping.

faqs.question: Is IB Gram affiliated with the IB Organization or with my child's school?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and has no official affiliation with the IB Organization, Cambridge International, Pearson Edexcel, or any individual school. Tutors are matched to support what a school is already teaching, working from the school's own IA task sheets, marking criteria and command terms, rather than delivering a separate or competing curriculum. This distinction matters because a tutor unfamiliar with your school's specific materials, however well-qualified generally, can end up teaching a version of the subject that doesn't line up with what's actually being assessed.

faqs.question: How far in advance of the May or November session should we start?
faqs.answer: There's no single right answer, since it depends on where the student currently stands, but earlier gives more room to work with. A student starting six to eight weeks before a mock has time to fix technique, not just cram content; a student starting the week before an exam session can only realistically focus on the highest-value gaps. Internal assessment deadlines, set individually by each school, often arrive earlier than families expect and are worth building a timeline around separately from the exam session itself, rather than treating everything as one deadline.

faqs.question: Can tutoring be paused or adjusted if our schedule changes mid-term?
faqs.answer: Yes. Session frequency and timing are agreed with the specific tutor and can be revisited if school timings, exams elsewhere, or family travel change what's realistic. A weekly plan can usually shift to fortnightly for a stretch, or intensify briefly before a mock, depending on the tutor's own availability at that point. This is worth raising directly with the tutor rather than letting sessions quietly lapse, since a plan that bends around a busy month is generally more sustainable than one abandoned when it stops fitting the calendar exactly as first set.

introSummary: IB Language Acquisition tutors help students learning a second language for the IB Diploma or Middle Years Programme, Language B or ab initio, from Grade 6 through Grade 12. IB Gram is a tutoring platform, not a school, and it matches families with tutors screened for subject depth, exam-board familiarity and the specific language and level a student needs. Lessons run online worldwide, in the family's own time zone, with home tutoring where a tutor happens to be local, and hybrid plans that mix both. Matching depends on level, language and schedule, not on which city you search from.

contentBlocks.heading: A Tuesday Night Language Session That Actually Fits the Timetable
contentBlocks.body:
It is 7:40 in the evening and a Grade 9 student still has a Language B Spanish oral to prepare for, along with homework in two other subjects, after a school day that started at 7:15 that morning. The parent tried one tutor from a local listing earlier this term who turned out to teach Language A literature, not Language Acquisition, and could not explain what an examiner means by developing a topic across familiar and unfamiliar contexts. That evening is not unusual. It repeats itself, in slightly different shapes, in households from Ghaziabad to Coimbatore, and in families running a full IB timetable from a city with no IB school of its own nearby.

IB Language Acquisition sits inside Group 2 of the Diploma Programme and also runs through the Middle Years Programme, covering ab initio and Language B at Standard and Higher Level, for students from Grade 6 through Grade 12. A tutor for it needs to know the gap between the receptive paper and the productive paper, understand how the Individual Oral is actually marked, and be fluent enough in the target language to correct pronunciation and register in real time, not just circle grammar mistakes on a worksheet.

IB Gram exists for this gap specifically. It matches a family to a tutor by language, level and IB familiarity first, and by city only where that happens to matter for travel. Sessions run online worldwide, in the family's own time zone, so a 7:40pm slot in one house is a convenient working hour somewhere else entirely.
