contentBlocks.heading: Signs of Real Progress by Week Four
contentBlocks.body:
Progress in IB Mathematics rarely looks dramatic in the first month, and a tutor who promises otherwise is telling you what you want to hear rather than what is true. A more honest marker, four weeks in, is whether the student can explain a method out loud without the tutor prompting each step — that shift, from copying a process to owning it, tends to show up before test scores do. Ask to see what the tutor has actually covered, not just a summary; a running list of topics, past-paper scores and specific weak points carries more information than a verbal assurance that things are going well.

It is worth being upfront about a limitation here: a tutor cannot compensate for a student who starts serious revision two months before the May session having missed most of Grade 11 content, and no amount of weekly tutoring rewrites that timeline honestly. What a good tutor can do in that situation is triage — decide which topics carry the most marks for the least additional study time — rather than attempt full coverage that was never realistic to begin with. Availability itself stays conditional throughout: a tutor's slots depend on their existing schedule, and a preferred time may need to shift as exam season approaches and demand for evening sessions increases across time zones.

Ask for a running record of topics and past-paper results

contentBlocks.heading: Starting With One Diagnostic Session
contentBlocks.body:
Starting is deliberately simple: tell IB Gram the course (Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation), the level, the grade, and the target exam session, and a shortlist is put together from tutors whose background actually matches, subject to availability and time zone. There is no obligation to commit beyond a first session, and that first session is designed to be genuinely diagnostic — a real past-paper question or a recent school test, worked through together, so both the tutor and the family know where things actually stand before any longer plan is agreed.

From there, sessions are scheduled around the family's own week, whether that is a single weekly online class or a more frequent hybrid pattern in the run-up to mocks. Fees and frequency depend on level, course and how much support is needed, and are discussed plainly before anything is booked — nothing here is presented as a fixed package because no two students need the same thing. If the first tutor is not the right fit, say so and a different one is arranged; the goal is a working relationship that survives past the first fortnight, not a booking.
items: Tell IB Gram the course, level, grade and exam session
First session is diagnostic: a real past paper or recent test
Fees discussed plainly before anything is booked
A different tutor arranged if the first match is wrong

faqs.question: Should my child take Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation?
faqs.answer: That decision usually sits with the school, based on the student's intended university subjects and prior performance, and a tutor should not override it lightly. Analysis and Approaches suits students heading toward maths-heavy subjects like engineering or economics and leans on algebraic technique and proof. Applications and Interpretation leans toward modelling, statistics and technology use, and suits students who find abstract manipulation harder than applied reasoning. If your child is already partway through the course and struggling, a tutor's first job is diagnosing whether the difficulty is the course choice itself or a specific topic gap — the two need very different responses.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help switch from Standard Level to Higher Level, or the other way round?
faqs.answer: A tutor can support a level change, but the school makes the final decision and usually has a cutoff date tied to the Diploma timeline. Moving up to Higher Level mid-course means covering vectors, more complex calculus and Paper 3 style questions that Standard Level students never see, which takes real catch-up time rather than a single session. Moving down is more straightforward but still needs a plan for whichever topics were only taught at the higher depth. Either way, a tutor should be told about the change immediately so the plan reflects the new syllabus rather than the old one.

faqs.question: Does online IB Mathematics tutoring actually work, or is home tutoring better?
faqs.answer: For this subject, online works well for most students because a shared whiteboard and screen-shared past papers cover almost everything a home session offers. It does depend on the student: younger learners in Grade 6 to Grade 8, or anyone who genuinely loses focus on a screen, often do better with a tutor physically in the room. Online also opens access to specialist AA Higher Level or Paper 3 support that may simply not exist as a home tutor within reasonable travel distance. The honest answer is that online is the better default, with home tutoring as a deliberate choice, not the assumed one.

faqs.question: What happens if there is no progress after a few weeks?
faqs.answer: First, look at what progress should even mean at four weeks — a shift in scores is a slower signal than a shift in whether the student can explain their own working. If neither is happening, ask the tutor directly what they have identified as the blocker; a vague answer is itself useful information. Sometimes the issue is genuinely the tutor-student fit rather than the plan, and IB Gram will arrange a different tutor rather than ask a family to persist through a mismatch. Occasionally the real issue is frequency — one session a week is not enough this close to an IA deadline or mock.

faqs.question: How much does an IB Mathematics tutor cost?
faqs.answer: Fees depend on the tutor's experience, whether the course is Standard or Higher Level, the mode chosen — online, home or hybrid — and how many sessions a week the plan needs. There is no single published rate because a Grade 7 revision session and a Higher Level Paper 3 specialist working with a Grade 12 student close to May are not comparable in either time or expertise required. IB Gram discusses fees plainly before any session is booked, tied to the specific tutor and plan proposed, rather than quoting a generic number that would not hold across every family's situation.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the Mathematics internal assessment?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is one of the more common requests. Help usually covers choosing a topic that is rich enough to explore but realistic to finish, structuring the exploration so it reads as genuine mathematical inquiry, and checking that notation and referencing meet the criteria the school will actually mark against. A tutor should never write or rewrite a student's IA — that crosses the academic honesty line schools take seriously — but reviewing drafts, asking probing questions and pointing out where the mathematics could go deeper is legitimate and often the difference between a mediocre and a strong exploration.

faqs.question: Is IB Gram affiliated with the IB Organization?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and has no affiliation with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel. Tutors are matched based on their own subject background and experience teaching IB Mathematics specifically, not through any relationship with the awarding body itself. This also means IB Gram does not set or influence syllabus content, IA requirements or exam dates — those remain entirely the school's and the IB Organization's domain, and any tutoring plan is built to fit within them rather than around them.

faqs.question: Can past papers really help this close to the exam?
faqs.answer: Yes, but only if they are used properly. Working through a past paper without checking the mark scheme line by line teaches a student to solve problems, not to score marks for solving them a particular way, and IB Mathematics rewards method marks specifically. A tutor's role close to the exam is often less about new content and more about tightening exam technique: showing sufficient working, managing time across Paper 1 and Paper 2, and recognising which questions to leave for later. Six weeks of properly reviewed past papers usually moves a score more than six weeks of new topics.

faqs.question: My child is in another country from most tutors — does time zone matter?
faqs.answer: It matters enough to settle upfront rather than assume it will work itself out. IB Gram runs sessions in the family's own time zone, and matching accounts for this before a tutor is even suggested, so a family in one part of the world is not offered a tutor whose only free hours are the middle of their night. Consistency matters more than exact overlap — a fixed weekly slot that both sides can actually keep is more useful than a theoretically perfect match that gets rescheduled every second week.

faqs.question: What if we want to change tutors partway through?
faqs.answer: That is normal and IB Gram treats it as normal, not as a complaint to justify. Fit matters as much as subject knowledge — a tutor who is technically strong but rushes, or under-explains, is not doing the job even if their own maths is faultless. Say plainly what is not working, whether that is pace, personality or communication, and a different tutor is arranged without the family needing to relitigate the whole matching process from scratch. It is worth raising the issue after two or three sessions rather than persisting for months hoping it resolves itself.

Analysis and Approaches suits students heading toward maths-heavy subjects like engineering or economics and leans on algebraic technique and proof. Applications and Interpretation leans toward modelling, statistics and technology use, and suits students who find abstract manipulation harder than applied reasoning. If your child is already partway through the course and struggling, a tutor's first job is diagnosing whether the difficulty is the course choice itself or a specific topic gap — the two need very different responses.

mainEntity.name: Can a tutor help switch from Standard Level to Higher Level, or the other way round?

acceptedAnswer.text: A tutor can support a level change, but the school makes the final decision and usually has a cutoff date tied to the Diploma timeline. Moving up to Higher Level mid-course means covering vectors, more complex calculus and Paper 3 style questions that Standard Level students never see, which takes real catch-up time rather than a single session. Moving down is more straightforward but still needs a plan for whichever topics were only taught at the higher depth. Either way, a tutor should be told about the change immediately so the plan reflects the new syllabus rather than the old one.

mainEntity.name: Does online IB Mathematics tutoring actually work, or is home tutoring better?

acceptedAnswer.text: For this subject, online works well for most students because a shared whiteboard and screen-shared past papers cover almost everything a home session offers. It does depend on the student: younger learners in Grade 6 to Grade 8, or anyone who genuinely loses focus on a screen, often do better with a tutor physically in the room. Online also opens access to specialist AA Higher Level or Paper 3 support that may simply not exist as a home tutor within reasonable travel distance. The honest answer is that online is the better default, with home tutoring as a deliberate choice, not the assumed one.

mainEntity.name: What happens if there is no progress after a few weeks?

acceptedAnswer.text: First, look at what progress should even mean at four weeks — a shift in scores is a slower signal than a shift in whether the student can explain their own working. If neither is happening, ask the tutor directly what they have identified as the blocker; a vague answer is itself useful information. Sometimes the issue is genuinely the tutor-student fit rather than the plan, and IB Gram will arrange a different tutor rather than ask a family to persist through a mismatch. Occasionally the real issue is frequency — one session a week is not enough this close to an IA deadline or mock.

mainEntity.name: How much does an IB Mathematics tutor cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fees depend on the tutor's experience, whether the course is Standard or Higher Level, the mode chosen — online, home or hybrid — and how many sessions a week the plan needs. There is no single published rate because a Grade 7 revision session and a Higher Level Paper 3 specialist working with a Grade 12 student close to May are not comparable in either time or expertise required. IB Gram discusses fees plainly before any session is booked, tied to the specific tutor and plan proposed, rather than quoting a generic number that would not hold across every family's situation.

mainEntity.name: Can a tutor help with the Mathematics internal assessment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and this is one of the more common requests. Help usually covers choosing a topic that is rich enough to explore but realistic to finish, structuring the exploration so it reads as genuine mathematical inquiry, and checking that notation and referencing meet the criteria the school will actually mark against. A tutor should never write or rewrite a student's IA — that crosses the academic honesty line schools take seriously — but reviewing drafts, asking probing questions and pointing out where the mathematics could go deeper is legitimate and often the difference between a mediocre and a strong exploration.

mainEntity.name: Is IB Gram affiliated with the IB Organization?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and has no affiliation with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel. Tutors are matched based on their own subject background and experience teaching IB Mathematics specifically, not through any relationship with the awarding body itself. This also means IB Gram does not set or influence syllabus content, IA requirements or exam dates — those remain entirely the school's and the IB Organization's domain, and any tutoring plan is built to fit within them rather than around them.

mainEntity.name: Can past papers really help this close to the exam?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but only if they are used properly. Working through a past paper without checking the mark scheme line by line teaches a student to solve problems, not to score marks for solving them a particular way, and IB Mathematics rewards method marks specifically. A tutor's role close to the exam is often less about new content and more about tightening exam technique: showing sufficient working, managing time across Paper 1 and Paper 2, and recognising which questions to leave for later. Six weeks of properly reviewed past papers usually moves a score more than six weeks of new topics.

mainEntity.name: My child is in another country from most tutors — does time zone matter?

acceptedAnswer.text: It matters enough to settle upfront rather than assume it will work itself out. IB Gram runs sessions in the family's own time zone, and matching accounts for this before a tutor is even suggested, so a family in one part of the world is not offered a tutor whose only free hours are the middle of their night. Consistency matters more than exact overlap — a fixed weekly slot that both sides can actually keep is more useful than a theoretically perfect match that gets rescheduled every second week.

mainEntity.name: What if we want to change tutors partway through?

acceptedAnswer.text: That is normal and IB Gram treats it as normal, not as a complaint to justify. Fit matters as much as subject knowledge — a tutor who is technically strong but rushes, or under-explains, is not doing the job even if their own maths is faultless. Say plainly what is not working, whether that is pace, personality or communication, and a different tutor is arranged without the family needing to relitigate the whole matching process from scratch. It is worth raising the issue after two or three sessions rather than persisting for months hoping it resolves itself.

contentBlocks.heading: What Should Actually Happen Before You Book an IB Physics Tutor
contentBlocks.body:
Before signing up for anything, most parents want one question answered plainly: will this actually help, given where my child is right now? That is the right question, and it is worth answering before price, before schedule, before anything else. An IB Physics tutor is only useful if the fit is right — the right level, HL or SL, the right stage of the Diploma, and a teaching style that matches how the student actually learns rather than how a marketing page describes tutoring in general.

IB Physics sits differently from a typical school subject. It is assessed against IB command terms, marked to detailed criteria, and taught through a concept-based approach that expects students to link ideas across topics rather than memorise formulas in isolation. A tutor who has only taught A-level or a national board physics course will often default to habits that do not transfer cleanly — different weighting on data-based questions, different expectations in the internal assessment, different exam technique for Paper 1, 2 and 3.

IB Gram exists to solve that specific matching problem for families anywhere, not to run a generic tuition centre. The platform connects students in Grade 6 through Grade 12 with tutors who teach specifically to the DP Physics syllabus, understand IA requirements and academic honesty rules, and can be reviewed against a student's actual gaps rather than a one-size profile. What that looks like in practice is covered block by block below.
items: HL vs SL fit checked before matching
Command-term and mark-scheme literacy required of tutors
Concept-based teaching, not memorised formulas
Grade 6 to Grade 12 covered under one platform

contentBlocks.heading: How DP Physics Fits Into the Wider IB Diploma Timeline
contentBlocks.body:
The IB Diploma Programme runs Physics at Higher Level or Standard Level across the final two years, but the tutoring most families ask about starts well before that. IB Gram covers Grade 6 to Grade 12, because a student who struggles with vectors or unit conversion in Grade 9 will struggle with DP mechanics two years later regardless of how good the DP-specific teaching is later on.

For students already in the Diploma, the working rhythm is set by two things: the school's own internal assessment deadlines, and the May or November examination session the student is registered for. These are not flexible dates a tutor can work around — they are fixed by the school and, ultimately, the IB Organization's calendar — so a sensible tutoring plan works backwards from them rather than treating every week the same. A student sitting the May session needs IA drafts finished and reviewed months earlier than the exam itself; a November-session student on a different school calendar needs a different pacing entirely.

HL and SL Physics share a common core but diverge in depth and in the additional HL-only content, so a tutor who only knows one level well can misjudge how much time a topic needs. Matching accounts for this rather than assuming any physics tutor can teach any level equally well.
items: Grade 6 to Grade 12 covered
HL and SL syllabus differences respected
Planning works backwards from May or November session
IA deadlines follow the school's own calendar, not a generic one

contentBlocks.heading: Where the Families Booking This Actually Are
contentBlocks.body:
IB Gram is not tied to one city or one country. Online lessons run worldwide, in the family's own time zone, which is the only way a Diploma Programme subject like Physics works for a genuinely international user base — an IB school in one country, a tutor with the right specialism somewhere else entirely, and a lesson time that has to suit both.

Even so, a meaningful share of enquiries for IB Physics still comes from a recognisable set of Indian cities — families based in Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Chennai, Coimbatore, Dehradun, Delhi, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Greater Noida among others, many at IB World Schools with a strong pull towards STEM subjects. For these families, home tutoring can be arranged where a tutor's travel route allows it, though this depends entirely on tutor availability in that specific city rather than a promise IB Gram can make in advance.

Everywhere else, and for a good share of families in these same cities too, online is simply the more practical option: no commute, no traffic-dependent scheduling, and access to a tutor whose specialism matches the exact syllabus rather than whoever happens to live nearby. Hybrid plans — mostly online with an occasional in-person session — are also possible where geography allows it.
items: Online worldwide, in the student's own time zone
Home tutoring subject to tutor availability by city
Enquiries include families in Delhi, Bangalore, Chennai and other IB hubs
Hybrid plans possible where a tutor is locally reachable

contentBlocks.heading: What the Physics Syllabus Actually Demands, Topic by Topic
contentBlocks.body:
Physics at Diploma level is not one uniform block of content — it moves from mechanics and thermal physics through waves, fields and electricity, into atomic, nuclear and particle physics, with Higher Level adding depth and extra content rather than entirely new subject areas. A tutor teaching to the syllabus needs to know not just the physics but how the IB weights each area across the written papers and the practical-based internal assessment.

The internal assessment is where most of the individual tutoring value shows up, because it is the one part of the subject with no fixed content: the student picks an investigation, and a tutor's job is to help sharpen the research question, check the method is genuinely testable in the time available, and read the criteria the way an examiner will — not just correct the physics. Weak IAs are rarely wrong on the science; they are usually vague on variables, light on uncertainty analysis, or answering a question broader than what was actually investigated.

Physics is also frequently paired with Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, since much of DP Physics — vectors, calculus-based kinematics, exponential decay — leans on mathematical tools the student may or may not have solidified yet. Where that gap exists, it is worth naming it early rather than letting it surface for the first time inside a physics lesson.
items: IA research question and variable control checked early
Paper 1, 2 and 3 weighting explained, not assumed known
Maths AA HL gaps flagged when they affect Physics
HL depth handled separately from SL core

contentBlocks.heading: IB World Schools, Cohorts, and Where IB Gram Sits Relative to Them
contentBlocks.body:
IB Gram does not teach inside any school and is not affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel — the tutoring runs alongside a student's own school, not in place of it or with any special access to it. That distinction matters more for Physics than it might for a humanities subject, because a lot of what a tutor needs to know — which topics the school has already covered, how the school's own teacher marks lab reports, what internal deadlines exist — comes from the student and parent, not from any partnership with the school.

Students come from IB World Schools of very different sizes and structures: some run large DP cohorts with several Physics teachers and well-established IA supervision, others run a small cohort where one teacher covers Physics across both HL and SL with less individual attention available per student. Tutoring tends to matter more in the second situation, simply because there is less slack in the system to catch a student who has quietly fallen behind.

Whichever the setup, a first session with an IB Gram tutor typically starts by understanding the school's own pace and expectations, so the tutoring adds to what the school is doing rather than teaching the same content twice or, worse, teaching it in a way that conflicts with how the school wants it presented.
items: No affiliation with the IB Organization, Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel
Tutoring supplements the school, does not replace it
Works with both large and small DP cohorts
First session maps the school's own pace before teaching begins

contentBlocks.heading: How a Tutor Actually Gets Matched to a Student
contentBlocks.body:
Matching starts with specifics, not a general request for 'a physics tutor'. The level (HL or SL), the current grade, the exam session the student is registered for, and what has already gone wrong or fallen behind — a shaky start on the IA, a specific topic like electromagnetic induction, general exam technique — all shape who gets suggested. A tutor whose strength is exam technique for a student two months from Paper 1 is a different match to one whose strength is building conceptual foundations for a Grade 9 student new to the subject.

Every tutor on the platform is checked for subject-specific qualification and teaching background before being offered for IB Physics specifically, not tutoring in general — familiarity with the syllabus, the command terms, and the criterion-based marking is treated as separate from general physics competence, because the two are not the same skill.

Once a match is proposed, the first session itself is diagnostic rather than instructional: working through recent test papers or IA drafts, identifying where marks are actually being lost, and agreeing what the next four weeks should focus on. By week four, a parent should be able to point to something concrete — a topic that has moved from shaky to solid, an IA draft that has gone from vague to specific, a mock score that has genuinely shifted — rather than a vague sense that lessons are happening.
items: Level, grade and exam session captured before matching
Subject-specific qualification and syllabus familiarity checked
First session is diagnostic, not a straight lesson
Four-week check-in against a concrete, named goal

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home or Hybrid — What Actually Suits Physics
contentBlocks.body:
Online tutoring is the default for most IB Physics bookings on the platform, and for a reason specific to this subject: the pool of tutors who genuinely know the DP syllabus at the right depth is not evenly spread across every city, so restricting the search to 'physics tutors within driving distance' usually means compromising on syllabus fit to get proximity. Online removes that trade-off — a student anywhere can be matched with a tutor whose specialism is exactly right, taught over video with a shared whiteboard for the diagrams and derivations that make up a large part of physics teaching.

Home tutoring still has a real place, particularly for younger students in Grade 6 to Grade 8 who benefit from someone physically present to hold attention and build study habits, and for whom the DP-specific specialism matters less than general foundation-building. It depends entirely on a tutor being available and reasonably placed to travel, which is a genuine constraint rather than a formality — it is worth saying plainly that this option simply will not exist in every case.

Hybrid plans — a weekly online lesson plus an occasional in-person session before a mock exam or major deadline — combine both reasonably well for families who want some face-to-face contact without giving up specialist matching. None of the three is universally correct; the right one depends on the student's age, the tutor pool available, and what the family can realistically sustain across a school year.
items: Online: widest access to syllabus-specific specialists
Home: better suited to younger, Grade 6-8 students
Home tutoring depends on tutor travel availability, not guaranteed
Hybrid: occasional in-person plus regular online sessions

contentBlocks.heading: What IB Gram Will Not Promise, and Why That Matters
contentBlocks.body:
No tutor, on this platform or any other, can promise a 7, a specific grade jump, or a guaranteed outcome, and it is worth being suspicious of anyone who does. What can be controlled is the process: whether the tutor actually knows the syllabus, whether sessions are structured around the student's actual gaps rather than a generic curriculum, and whether progress is checked honestly rather than assumed.

A fair limitation to state plainly: tutoring started a few weeks before a May or November session cannot substitute for two years of consistent classroom learning. It can sharpen exam technique, fix specific misunderstandings, and improve IA presentation — all of which move marks — but it cannot rebuild an entire subject from a cold start in six weeks. Families in that position are better served by an honest conversation about what is realistically achievable than by a tutor who says yes to everything.

Where tutoring does work reliably is in the space between those extremes: a student broadly on track but losing marks to avoidable things — sloppy uncertainty analysis, a shaky grip on one HL-only topic, exam technique that does not match how IB Physics papers are actually structured. That is a solvable problem, and it is the problem most families booking a tutor are actually trying to solve, whether or not they have named it that way to themselves yet.
items: No promised grades or guaranteed outcomes
Late-start tutoring has real limits, stated honestly
Best suited to fixing specific, identifiable gaps
Progress checked against real work, not assumed

contentBlocks.heading: What Gets Checked Before a Tutor Is Ever Suggested
contentBlocks.body:
Before a tutor is offered for an IB Physics match, several things are checked rather than taken on trust. Academic background is verified — a physics-relevant degree or equivalent qualification, not an adjacent science treated as close enough. Teaching experience specific to the IB Diploma is checked separately from general tutoring experience, because familiarity with command terms, criterion-related marking and academic honesty expectations is not something a strong A-level or national-board tutor automatically has.

Where possible, exam-board familiarity is verified through the tutor's own history — years actually spent teaching or examining DP Physics, exposure to real past papers and mark schemes, and comfort with how the IA is assessed against the criteria rather than against a generic lab-report rubric. This matters because IA criteria change across syllabus revisions, and a tutor working from outdated assumptions can genuinely cost a student marks.

None of this is visible to a parent unless they ask, so it is worth asking directly: how long has this tutor taught DP Physics specifically, at what level, and how many IAs have they actually supervised through to a final grade. A platform that has done this vetting properly will have a straightforward answer; one that has not will talk around the question.
items: Physics-relevant qualification verified, not an adjacent subject
IB-specific teaching experience checked separately from general tutoring
Familiarity with current IA criteria, not an outdated syllabus version
Parents encouraged to ask about specific IA supervision history

contentBlocks.heading: Starting the Process, Step by Step
contentBlocks.body:
Getting started does not require a long commitment or an upfront exam-level decision. The usual first step is a short conversation about the student's current level — HL or SL, which grade, which exam session — followed by a proposed tutor match based on that information rather than a generic sign-up form. There is no obligation to continue past a first session if the fit is not right, and saying so plainly is more useful to a parent than pretending mismatches never happen.

From there, a first session is diagnostic: recent test papers, an IA draft if one exists, or simply a conversation about where marks are being lost. That session gives both the tutor and the family a realistic sense of what four, eight and twelve weeks of consistent work could look like, rather than a vague promise of improvement. Scheduling is arranged around the family's own time zone and the school's calendar, particularly around IA deadlines and mock exam dates, since those are the fixed points everything else works backwards from.

Changing tutors, if the fit turns out to be wrong after a genuine attempt, is a normal part of the process rather than a failure on anyone's part — subject knowledge and personal teaching style are different things, and occasionally the first match does not land even when the qualifications are right on paper.
items: Start with a short conversation on level and exam session
First session is diagnostic, not a sales pitch
Scheduling built around time zone and school IA deadlines
Switching tutors is normal if the fit is wrong

faqs.question: How is IB Physics tutoring different from normal physics tuition?
faqs.answer: IB Physics is assessed differently from a typical school or national-board physics course — through command terms, criterion-related marking, and an internally assessed investigation with no fixed topic. Ordinary physics tuition often focuses on solving problems correctly; IB Physics tuition also has to focus on how those answers are structured, since IB examiners mark against specific criteria rather than just checking a final number. A tutor without DP-specific experience can teach the physics correctly and still leave a student losing marks on presentation, uncertainty analysis, or how a Paper 3 data-based question is approached.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring actually work for a subject like Physics?
faqs.answer: It works for most students, with one caveat: physics leans heavily on diagrams, derivations and worked graphs, so the online setup needs a shared whiteboard or annotation tool, not just a video call. Where that is in place, online tutoring generally performs as well as in-person for DP Physics, and it opens access to tutors with the right specialism regardless of where they live. Students who need more hands-on redirection to stay focused — often younger students — sometimes do better with home tutoring instead, which is a fair trade-off to weigh honestly rather than assume online always wins.

faqs.question: What does IB Physics tutoring cost?
faqs.answer: Fees depend on the tutor's experience, whether lessons are HL or SL, and whether the arrangement is online, home or hybrid — home tutoring generally costs more once a tutor's travel time is factored in. Rather than quote a single figure that would not hold across very different situations, IB Gram works out a fee once a specific tutor and schedule are proposed, so a family is comparing an actual quote against their own budget rather than a marketing number. It is fair to ask for this upfront before committing to sessions.

faqs.question: What happens if the first tutor is not a good fit?
faqs.answer: Switching is straightforward and treated as a normal outcome, not a complaint that needs justifying at length. Subject knowledge and teaching style are different things — a tutor can know DP Physics thoroughly and still not suit how a particular student learns best. After a genuine attempt, usually a handful of sessions, a family can ask for a different match, informed by what specifically did not work the first time, which usually improves the second match considerably, and there is no penalty for asking.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help specifically with the Physics internal assessment?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is often where individual tutoring adds the most value, because the IA has no fixed content for a tutor to simply re-teach. Support typically covers sharpening the research question so it is genuinely testable in the time available, checking that variables and uncertainty analysis are handled the way the criteria expect, and reviewing drafts against the assessment criteria rather than general scientific writing standards. A tutor cannot write or substantially rewrite the IA — academic honesty rules do not allow that — but can guide the student toward a stronger version of their own work.

faqs.question: My child is switching into IB Physics from an A-level or national board course. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: It is manageable but worth naming early rather than discovering mid-year. The core physics content overlaps substantially, but IB Physics structures assessment differently — command terms, criterion-based marking, and the internal assessment are unfamiliar territory even for a student who understands the science well. Tutoring in this situation often focuses less on new content and more on translating existing knowledge into how the IB actually wants it presented and marked, which is a narrower and faster job than teaching physics from scratch.

faqs.question: Is IB Gram affiliated with the IB Organization or with any school?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and has no affiliation with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, and no partnership with any specific school. Tutors are matched to work alongside a student's existing school and syllabus, using publicly available IB Physics curriculum information and past papers, not any privileged access. This distinction matters because it means the tutoring adapts to whatever a particular school is doing, rather than assuming every DP Physics cohort is taught identically.

faqs.question: How does scheduling work across different time zones?
faqs.answer: Sessions are arranged around the family's own time zone rather than the tutor's, since online tutoring is worldwide by design. In practice this means confirming a recurring weekly slot that suits the student's school timings and homework load, then adjusting around IA deadlines or mock exam periods when extra sessions are useful. Families working with a tutor in a very different time zone should expect slightly less flexibility for last-minute rescheduling, simply because overlapping available hours are narrower — a reasonable trade-off for the wider choice of specialist tutors it opens up.

faqs.question: What should actually change in the first four weeks of tutoring?
faqs.answer: A parent should be able to point to something specific: a topic that has moved from confused to confident, an IA draft that reads more precisely than the first version, or a mock question type the student can now approach without hesitation. If nothing concrete has shifted by then, that is worth raising directly with the tutor rather than assuming more time will fix it — four weeks is enough to see direction, even if it is not enough to see a full grade change yet.

faqs.question: Is there a minimum commitment, like a term or a full year?
faqs.answer: No fixed minimum is required upfront. Most families start with a short block of sessions to see whether the match works before agreeing to anything longer, and scheduling can be adjusted as the exam session approaches or as a student's needs change — more frequent sessions before IA deadlines or mocks, fewer during quieter periods. What matters more than the length of commitment is whether the sessions are actually being used consistently, since sporadic tutoring rarely moves marks much regardless of how many months it runs for.

faqs.question: What if my child is preparing for the November session instead of May?
faqs.answer: The subject content is identical, but the calendar around it is not — school terms, mock exam timing and IA deadlines for a November cohort often run on a different rhythm than the more commonly discussed May session. A tutor working with a November-session student needs to plan backwards from that specific date rather than defaulting to a generic May-centred timeline, which is a detail worth confirming explicitly when a match is first proposed.

Tutors are matched to work alongside a student's existing school and syllabus, using publicly available IB Physics curriculum information and past papers, not any privileged access. This distinction matters because it means the tutoring adapts to whatever a particular school is doing, rather than assuming every DP Physics cohort is taught identically.

mainEntity.name: How does scheduling work across different time zones?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sessions are arranged around the family's own time zone rather than the tutor's, since online tutoring is worldwide by design. In practice this means confirming a recurring weekly slot that suits the student's school timings and homework load, then adjusting around IA deadlines or mock exam periods when extra sessions are useful. Families working with a tutor in a very different time zone should expect slightly less flexibility for last-minute rescheduling, simply because overlapping available hours are narrower — a reasonable trade-off for the wider choice of specialist tutors it opens up.

mainEntity.name: What should actually change in the first four weeks of tutoring?

acceptedAnswer.text: A parent should be able to point to something specific: a topic that has moved from confused to confident, an IA draft that reads more precisely than the first version, or a mock question type the student can now approach without hesitation. If nothing concrete has shifted by then, that is worth raising directly with the tutor rather than assuming more time will fix it — four weeks is enough to see direction, even if it is not enough to see a full grade change yet.

mainEntity.name: Is there a minimum commitment, like a term or a full year?

acceptedAnswer.text: No fixed minimum is required upfront. Most families start with a short block of sessions to see whether the match works before agreeing to anything longer, and scheduling can be adjusted as the exam session approaches or as a student's needs change — more frequent sessions before IA deadlines or mocks, fewer during quieter periods. What matters more than the length of commitment is whether the sessions are actually being used consistently, since sporadic tutoring rarely moves marks much regardless of how many months it runs for.

mainEntity.name: What if my child is preparing for the November session instead of May?

acceptedAnswer.text: The subject content is identical, but the calendar around it is not — school terms, mock exam timing and IA deadlines for a November cohort often run on a different rhythm than the more commonly discussed May session. A tutor working with a November-session student needs to plan backwards from that specific date rather than defaulting to a generic May-centred timeline, which is a detail worth confirming explicitly when a match is first proposed.

finalCta: If your child needs an IB Physics tutor who actually teaches to the DP syllabus — HL or SL, Grade 6 through Grade 12 — start with a short conversation about their current level and exam session. IB Gram matches from there, worldwide, online or hybrid, with availability always subject to tutor schedules and location.

introSummary: Parents searching for IB Sciences tutors are usually trying to fix a specific gap: a predicted grade that doesn't match the target university offer, an IA that stalled, or a Physics or Chemistry topic that never quite clicked. IB Gram matches students in Grade 6 to Grade 12 with subject tutors who teach Biology, Chemistry and Physics at Higher Level or Standard Level, understand IB command terms and criterion-related assessment, and plan around the May and November examination sessions. Tutoring runs online worldwide, in the family's own time zone, with home and hybrid options depending on tutor availability.

contentBlocks.heading: The Gap Between a Predicted Grade and a Final Grade
contentBlocks.body: Every IB family eventually asks the same question in a different form: why did the final grade come in lower than the predicted grade, and what would have closed that gap earlier. In Sciences, Biology, Chemistry and Physics, the gap usually isn't about talent. It's about exam technique under IB conditions: reading a command term correctly, showing working the way a Paper 2 mark scheme rewards, or managing a six-mark data-analysis question with the same calm a student would bring to a five-mark recall question. A predicted grade is a teacher's professional estimate, made months before the exam, based on classwork, mocks and coursework. The final grade is set by external examiners against IB grade boundaries that shift slightly each session. Between the two sits real, coachable work: past-paper practice scored against the actual mark scheme, IA feedback that goes beyond a single read-through, and a study plan built around the student's weakest topic rather than their favourite one. IB Gram matches students from Grade 6 through Grade 12 with tutors who teach Sciences at Higher Level and Standard Level, and who work backward from the exam session the student is actually sitting rather than from a generic syllabus overview. Some students need six weeks before a mock. Others start in Grade 6 and simply need steady, patient grounding in scientific method before IB's assessment style becomes relevant at all.
items: Predicted grades are set by the school; final grades by external IB examiners
Paper 2 and Paper 3 mark schemes reward method, not just the right number
Grade 6 to Grade 12 covers pre-DP grounding through final exam revision
May and November sessions each carry their own grade boundaries

contentBlocks.heading: How a Family Gets Matched With a Sciences Tutor
contentBlocks.body: The process starts with specifics, not a form asking for a favourite subject. A parent tells IB Gram the student's grade, whether the school runs Biology, Chemistry or Physics at Higher Level or Standard Level, which exam session the student is preparing for, and what has actually gone wrong so far, a weak IA draft, shaky Paper 3 data-response technique, or simply a syllabus that moved faster than the student could absorb it. That detail decides who gets shortlisted, not the other way round. IB Gram checks a tutor's academic background, subject depth and familiarity with IB's command terms and criterion-related assessment before they're offered to any family; a tutor who has only taught a national board syllabus is not treated as equivalent to one who has actually marked IA drafts against IB criteria. The family reviews a short shortlist rather than one default assignment, and a first session is used to confirm fit before committing to a term of lessons, checking the tutor's approach against how the student actually learns, not just their qualifications on paper. If the match is wrong, it gets flagged and replaced rather than persisted with out of politeness. Ongoing check-ins, typically every few weeks, track whether the plan is producing the kind of measurable movement, clearer working, faster recall, fewer careless marks lost, that a parent can actually see rather than take on trust.
items: Tell IB Gram the grade, level and exam session before browsing tutors
Tutors are checked for subject depth and IB assessment familiarity, not general teaching background
A first session confirms fit before any term commitment
Mismatches are replaced, not carried through out of courtesy
Check-ins every few weeks track real, visible progress

contentBlocks.heading: Where Biology, Chemistry and Physics Sit Inside IB
contentBlocks.body: IB Sciences isn't one syllabus; it changes shape as a student moves up the programme. In the Middle Years Programme, roughly Grade 6 to Grade 10, sciences are taught as an integrated subject building toward the MYP's criteria-based assessment, a different skill from a straightforward test-and-mark system, and one that surprises parents used to percentage scores. By the Diploma Programme, Sciences becomes Group 4: a student chooses Biology, Chemistry, Physics, or occasionally more than one, at Higher Level or Standard Level, and the choice matters more than families often realise going in. HL adds extra content and a harder Paper 1 and Paper 2, and dropping from HL to SL mid-course is possible in principle but rarely painless once a school year is underway. Every Group 4 subject carries an internal assessment component and contributes to the collaborative Group 4 project, alongside the external Paper 1, Paper 2 and Paper 3 exams sat in the May or November session. A tutor who only knows the content but not this structure will misjudge how much time a student actually needs for IA write-ups versus content revision. IB Gram's Sciences tutors work across this full Grade 6 to Grade 12 range, which means a family doesn't need to switch tutor every time a student moves from MYP sciences into DP Biology HL, provided the same tutor's subject depth still covers the new level.
items: MYP (roughly Grade 6-10): integrated sciences, criteria-based assessment
DP Group 4: Biology, Chemistry, Physics at HL or SL
Internal assessment plus the collaborative Group 4 project
Paper 1, Paper 2 and Paper 3 in the May or November session
HL-to-SL switches are possible but rarely smooth mid-year

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home or Hybrid: Matching the Mode to the Student
contentBlocks.body: Online tutoring is the default for one plain reason: it opens up the full pool of specialist Sciences tutors regardless of which city a family lives in, and it runs in the family's own time zone rather than forcing lessons around a tutor's local clock. For a Grade 11 student needing a specific HL Physics tutor with strong IA supervision experience, that access matters more than proximity ever would. Home tutoring works differently, and it isn't automatically the better option, it depends on tutor availability in that particular city and, honestly, on whether a family is willing to trade subject-specialist choice for in-person presence. Younger students, especially those still building basic scientific method in MYP, often benefit from someone physically in the room checking their notebook and lab write-ups line by line; a screen doesn't always catch a habit forming badly. Hybrid plans split the difference: a weekly online session for content and past-paper drilling, paired with an occasional in-person session timed around a mock or IA deadline, where a tutor happens to be within reasonable travel of the family. None of these is universally correct. A family choosing purely on convenience, without weighing what the student actually responds to, tends to switch modes twice before settling, better to be honest about the trade-off up front than to discover it after a term.
items: Online: full choice of specialist tutors, sessions in the family's own time zone
Home: depends on tutor availability nearby, suits younger MYP learners
Hybrid: weekly online plus occasional in-person around a mock or IA deadline
No single mode is right for every student or subject

contentBlocks.heading: What Biology, Chemistry and Physics Tutoring Actually Covers
contentBlocks.body: Good Sciences tutoring isn't a running commentary on the textbook. It's built around four things that actually move a grade: IA and coursework planning, past-paper practice, mark-scheme technique, and mock preparation, tied together by weekly goal setting rather than an open-ended 'let's see how it goes' approach. IA planning starts early, ideally a term before the deadline, not the week before, because a strong Biology or Chemistry IA needs a testable research question, a realistic data collection plan given the equipment a school actually has, and enough draft-and-feedback cycles to fix a flawed methodology before it's too late to redesign. Past-paper practice matters more in Sciences than almost any other IB subject group, because Paper 2 and Paper 3 reward a specific way of showing working: units carried through every line, correct significant figures, and answers that engage with the command term actually used rather than a memorised definition. Mark-scheme technique is a skill in itself, a student can know the content and still lose marks by writing a technically-correct answer that a marker can't credit against the published scheme. Mock preparation works backwards from the exam date: content review first, then timed paper practice, then a final pass focused only on the topics still costing marks. Weekly goals keep this honest, a specific, checkable target each week rather than a vague sense of covering more content.
items: IA and coursework planning starting a term ahead, not the week before
Past-paper practice scored against the real mark scheme
Mark-scheme technique: making an answer creditable, not just correct
Mock preparation working backward from the exam date
Weekly, checkable goals instead of open-ended content review

contentBlocks.heading: Different Schools, Different Sciences Programmes, One Consistent Approach
contentBlocks.body: IB Sciences is taught in schools on every continent, and no two run it quite the same way. Some schools front-load Group 4 content early in Grade 11 and leave the second year mostly for revision and the IA; others spread content evenly across both years and leave IA work later, which changes how much a tutor needs to compress into the final term. Lab access varies enormously too, a school with a well-equipped Chemistry lab lets students collect their own IA data, while a school with more limited facilities often pushes students toward secondary-data or simulation-based investigations instead, and a tutor who assumes one approach when the school uses the other will waste a session correcting a wrong assumption. Assessment weighting between internal and external components also differs slightly by subject and by which exam session a school follows. None of this is something IB Gram can standardise, because it isn't IB Gram's syllabus to set, the platform matches families with tutors, it does not run a school or set curriculum. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and is not officially affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, and it has no relationship with any individual school beyond what a family and tutor establish directly. What a tutor can and should do, wherever the school is, is ask early which structure the student's school actually follows before building a study plan around the wrong one.
items: IA data collection depends heavily on a school's lab access
Group 4 content pacing varies, some schools front-load, others spread it evenly
Internal vs external assessment weighting differs slightly by school and session
IB Gram is independent, not affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel

contentBlocks.heading: Reaching Students Across Cities and Time Zones
contentBlocks.body: IB Gram works with families wherever the student's school happens to be, because a Sciences tutor's value has very little to do with which city they're based in once the lesson moves online. A family in one time zone can be matched with a Physics HL specialist based somewhere else entirely, and the lesson still lands at a sensible hour for the student rather than the tutor. Even so, home and hybrid tutoring only work where a tutor is genuinely nearby, and availability for in-person sessions varies by city, sometimes there's a strong bench of Sciences tutors within reasonable travel, sometimes there isn't, and it would be dishonest to promise otherwise. IB Gram's tutor network includes people based in and around hubs such as Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Chennai, Coimbatore, Dehradun, Delhi, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Greater Noida, among many other cities worldwide, so a family near any of these has a reasonable chance of finding a nearby option if home or hybrid tutoring is what actually suits the student. For everyone else, online remains the default, and it is not a downgrade, it is simply the mode that gives access to the right subject specialist rather than the nearest one. A parent deciding between modes should ask the practical question first: does this student need someone physically present, or does the student mainly need the right tutor at the right time, in whichever city that tutor happens to sit in.
items: Home and hybrid tutoring depend on tutor availability in the family's city
Hub cities with an active tutor bench include Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Delhi, Chennai and Dehradun, among others worldwide
Online tutoring removes the city constraint entirely for subject-specialist matching
The right question is fit and specialism first, location second

contentBlocks.heading: What IB Gram Won't Promise, and What It Will
contentBlocks.body: No tutor, however good, can guarantee a 7 or a specific grade jump, and any platform claiming otherwise is telling a parent what they want to hear rather than what's true. IB Sciences grades depend on the student's starting point, the school's own teaching, how much time is genuinely available before the exam session, and factors no tutor controls, like exam-day nerves or a harder-than-usual paper. What IB Gram can be honest about is process: every Sciences tutor is checked for relevant academic background and subject depth before being offered to a family, not simply for a general willingness to teach. That check looks at whether the tutor's own qualification and experience sit in the actual subject and level being requested, Biology HL supervision experience is not interchangeable with general secondary-school Biology teaching, and IB Gram treats that distinction as a real one, not paperwork. Availability is described honestly too: tutoring can be reviewed and adjusted depending on level and schedule, home tutoring is subject to which tutors are actually near a family, and a session cadence that suits a Grade 7 student building fundamentals looks nothing like the twice-weekly intensity a Grade 12 student needs six weeks from a May exam. A parent who hears vague reassurance instead of this kind of specific, checkable detail should ask more questions before committing, on any platform, not only this one.
items: No guaranteed grades or score jumps, ever
Tutors checked for subject-and-level match, not general teaching willingness
Availability described honestly: subject to schedule, level and tutor location
Session cadence differs for a Grade 7 student versus a Grade 12 student near exams

contentBlocks.heading: What Gets Checked Before a Tutor Ever Meets a Student
contentBlocks.body: Before a Sciences tutor is shown to any family, IB Gram reviews their academic qualifications, subject background and prior teaching or tutoring experience specific to Biology, Chemistry or Physics, along with familiarity with IB's command terms, criterion-related assessment and the general shape of the Group 4 syllabus at HL and SL. This isn't a one-time check that gets filed away; a tutor's suitability is reassessed against each new family's specific request, because a tutor who is excellent for Grade 12 Chemistry HL exam revision may not be the right fit for a Grade 6 student who needs patient, foundational scientific-method work instead. A first session is treated as diagnostic, not decorative: the tutor works through where the student actually is against where the syllabus expects them to be, identifies which of IA planning, past-paper technique or core content is the more urgent gap, and sets a specific plan rather than a general promise to cover the syllabus. Around four weeks in, a parent should expect to see something concrete, improved working shown on practice questions, a clearer IA draft, faster and more accurate recall on topics that were previously shaky, not just a tutor's own assurance that things are going well. If that concrete movement isn't visible by then, the honest next step is a conversation about adjusting the plan or the tutor, not persisting for the sake of continuity.
items: Academic background and subject-level match checked before any introduction
First session is diagnostic: it maps the real gap, not a generic overview
Reassessed per request, a great Grade 12 tutor may not suit a Grade 6 student
Week-four check: concrete evidence expected, not just reassurance

contentBlocks.heading: Starting With One Focused Conversation
contentBlocks.body: The families who get the most out of Sciences tutoring are usually the ones who start with a specific problem rather than a general search for a good tutor. That means naming the actual grade, the exact subject and level, Biology, Chemistry or Physics, HL or SL, the exam session being prepared for, and the honest reason things haven't gone to plan so far, whether that's an IA stuck at draft stage, careless errors on Paper 1, or a topic the student has quietly avoided for two terms. IB Gram uses that detail to shortlist tutors whose subject depth and experience actually match the request, rather than offering the first available person. There's no obligation attached to asking; a parent can review a shortlist, ask questions about a tutor's background, and decide the mode, online, home or hybrid, before any lesson is booked. For a family with more time before the exam, a slower, foundation-building pace usually works better than intensive drilling started too early and burned out by the time it matters. For a family closer to a mock or a final exam, the plan looks different again: focused, past-paper-heavy, and unapologetically narrow. Either way, the starting point is the same, a clear, specific ask, matched against a tutor who has actually done this particular kind of work before, not a general promise that everything will be fine.
items: Name the exact subject, level and exam session before browsing tutors
Review a shortlist and ask about background before committing
Choose online, home or hybrid based on what the student needs, not convenience
Foundation-building pace for students with time; focused revision for students near an exam

faqs.question: How much does IB Sciences tutoring cost?
faqs.answer: Fees depend on the subject, the level, Higher Level tuition generally needs more tutor preparation than Standard Level, the student's grade, and how experienced the tutor is, so IB Gram doesn't quote one fixed number upfront. A parent gets a cost estimate once the shortlist is built around the actual subject and exam session, which lets the fee reflect the real scope of work: IA supervision costs more tutor time than straightforward content revision, for instance. It's worth asking for a breakdown by session type before committing, so home, online and any exam-intensive blocks are priced separately and clearly.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring actually work for a lab-based subject like Chemistry or Biology?
faqs.answer: It works for most of what determines a Sciences grade, content mastery, past-paper technique, IA feedback and mark-scheme practice, none of which require a physical lab. What online tutoring can't replace is hands-on practical skill, but that's the school's job through timetabled practicals, not a tutor's. A good online tutor instead works from the student's own practical write-ups and data, correcting method and analysis rather than repeating the experiment. Students who struggle mainly with exam technique and written analysis, which is most students by Grade 11, tend to do very well with this format.

faqs.question: What if the tutor turns out to be the wrong fit for my child?
faqs.answer: Say so early rather than waiting out a term hoping it improves. IB Gram treats a mismatch as something to fix, not something the family has to manage alone, a different tutor can be shortlisted using exactly the same detail from the original request, so it doesn't mean starting the process from scratch. Signs worth acting on include a student who stops engaging, sessions that feel like a lecture rather than a two-way check of understanding, or four weeks passing with no visible change in practice-paper performance. None of that is disloyalty to the tutor; it's just data.

faqs.question: Should my child take Sciences at Higher Level or Standard Level?
faqs.answer: That decision usually belongs with the school and the student's intended university direction more than with a tutor, since HL carries extra content and is expected for many Sciences-heavy degree offers. Where a tutor genuinely helps is in the months after the choice is made: confirming the student can actually handle HL's pace before it's too late to reconsider, or making sure an SL choice isn't quietly under-ambitious for a student capable of more. A tutor who has taught both levels can speak to the real difference in workload, which is larger than the syllabus documents suggest.

faqs.question: My child is only in Grade 7, is it too early for a Sciences tutor?
faqs.answer: Not at all, though the kind of tutoring should look different from Grade 12 exam coaching. At Grade 7, the goal is usually steady grounding in scientific method, confident lab-report writing and comfort with MYP's criteria-based assessment, not past-paper drilling for an exam years away. Starting this early, when there's no pressure, tends to build habits, careful units, structured written answers, curiosity about why an experiment worked, that make the DP years considerably less stressful later. It's a different product from exam tutoring, and a good tutor will say so rather than treating every grade the same.

faqs.question: What happens if there's no real progress after a few months?
faqs.answer: First, that should show up early, a four-week check is built into the process precisely so it doesn't take months to notice. If practice-paper scores, IA quality or basic recall genuinely haven't moved, the honest options are adjusting the plan, changing frequency, or changing the tutor, roughly in that order. Sometimes the issue isn't the tutor at all, a student needing more session time than the plan allows, or a school pace the tutoring hasn't been aligned to yet. Either way, the response should be a specific change, not vague reassurance to keep going.

faqs.question: Is IB Gram affiliated with the IB Organization or my child's school?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and has no official affiliation with the IB Organization, Cambridge International, Pearson Edexcel, or any individual school. It doesn't set the syllabus, run assessments or represent any school's curriculum team, it matches families with tutors who understand IB's structure and requirements. That distinction matters practically: a tutor's job is to support the school's teaching and the IA process the school has set, not to substitute for it or claim authority the school hasn't given it.

faqs.question: How does IA support actually work, does the tutor write it for the student?
faqs.answer: No, and any tutor offering to write or substantially rewrite a student's IA is a serious academic-honesty risk that could cost the student the mark entirely. What proper IA support looks like is feedback: checking the research question is testable, that the methodology is realistic given the school's equipment, and that the analysis engages properly with the data rather than just describing it. A tutor reviews drafts and flags weaknesses; the student does the actual thinking and writing. That boundary matters more in Sciences IAs than almost anywhere else in the Diploma.

faqs.question: Can tutoring be paused or adjusted around exam sessions and school terms?
faqs.answer: Yes, session frequency is meant to flex around the May and November exam sessions and each school's own internal deadlines, rather than running at one fixed pace all year. A student six weeks from a mock typically needs more frequent, narrower sessions than one in the middle of a school term with no immediate deadline. Families can ask to adjust cadence at any point rather than sticking to an initial schedule that no longer fits, and a reasonable tutor will expect and welcome that conversation rather than resist it.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram only work with students in one country?
faqs.answer: No, IB Sciences tutoring through IB Gram is available to families worldwide, with online lessons run in the student's own time zone regardless of where the tutor is based. Home and hybrid tutoring depend on a tutor's actual proximity, which varies by city, but online access to a properly matched subject specialist doesn't depend on geography at all. A family relocating mid-programme, a common IB scenario, can keep the same tutor online even after moving to a different city or country, which keeps continuity through an otherwise disruptive transition.
